(b) Evidence as to numbers and types of valid and justifiable complaints to the Commissioner against an insurance company, and the Commissioner’s complaint experience with other insurance companies writing similar lines of insurance shall be admissible in evidence in an administrative or judicial proceeding brought under this section. (c) If it is found, after notice and an opportunity to be heard, that an insurance company has violated this section, each instance of noncompliance with paragraph (a) may be treated as a separate violation of this section and shall be considered sufficient cause for the suspension or revocation of the company’s certificate of authority.
explanation: The Code prohibits refusal to settle a covered claim without just cause and specifies unfair practices. The listed behavior becomes “unfair claim settlement practices” when done without just cause and frequently enough to indicate a general business practice—not merely because one isolated communication was imperfect.

verbatim: The proceeds of a life insurance policy shall be paid immediately upon maturity of the policy, unless such proceeds are made payable in installments or as an annuity, in which case the installments, or annuities shall be paid as they become due: Provided, however, That in the case of a policy maturing by the death of the insured, the proceeds thereof shall be paid within sixty (60) days after presentation of the claim and filing of the proof of death of the insured. Refusal or failure to pay the claim within the time prescribed herein will entitle the beneficiary to collect interest on the proceeds of the policy for the duration of the delay at the rate of twice the ceiling prescribed by the Monetary Board, unless such failure or refusal to pay is based on the ground that the claim is fraudulent. The proceeds of the policy maturing by the death of the insured payable to the beneficiary shall include the discounted value of all premiums paid in advance of their due dates, but are not due and payable at maturity.
explanation: Life-insurance proceeds are due immediately at maturity, subject to the payment structure stated in the policy. Where the policy matures by death, the statutory period is 60 days after presentation of the claim and filing of proof of death. The section provides interest for unjustified delay, subject to its fraud exception.

verbatim: The amount of any loss or damage for which an insurer may be liable, under any policy other than life insurance policy, shall be paid within thirty (30) days after proof of loss is received by the insurer and ascertainment of the loss or damage is made either by agreement between the insured and the insurer or by arbitration; but if such ascertainment is not had or made within sixty (60) days after such receipt by the insurer of the proof of loss, then the loss or damage shall be paid within ninety (90) days after such receipt. Refusal or failure to pay the loss or damage within the time prescribed herein will entitle the assured to collect interest on the proceeds of the policy for the duration of the delay at the rate of twice the ceiling prescribed by the Monetary Board, unless such failure or refusal to pay is based on the ground that the claim is fraudulent.
explanation: For non-life insurance, the usual deadline is 30 days after proof of loss and ascertainment of the amount by agreement or arbitration. If the amount is not ascertained within 60 days after proof of loss, the section sets a 90-day outer timeline measured from receipt of proof of loss. It also provides interest for delay, subject to the statutory fraud exception.

verbatim: In case of any litigation for the enforcement of any policy or contract of insurance, it shall be the duty of the Commissioner or the Court, as the case may be, to make a finding as to whether the payment of the claim of the insured has been unreasonably denied or withheld; and in the affirmative case, the insurance company shall be adjudged to pay damages which shall consist of attorney’s fees and other expenses incurred by the insured person by reason of such unreasonable denial or withholding of payment plus interest of twice the ceiling prescribed by the Monetary Board of the amount of the claim due the insured, from the date following the time prescribed in Section 248 or in Section 249, as the case may be, until the claim is fully satisfied: Provided, That failure to pay any such claim within the time prescribed in said sections shall be considered prima facie evidence of unreasonable delay in payment.
explanation: In litigation to enforce a policy, the Commissioner or court must determine whether payment was unreasonably denied or withheld. If so, the insurer may be liable for attorney’s fees, other reasonable expenses caused by the delay, and the statutory interest. Missing the payment deadlines is prima facie evidence of unreasonable delay, not necessarily the only evidence relevant to the final ruling.

verbatim: It is unlawful to: (a) Present or cause to be presented any fraudulent claim for the payment of a loss under a contract of insurance; and (b) Fraudulently prepare, make or subscribe any writing with intent to present or use the same, or to allow it to be presented in support of any such claim. Any person who violates this section shall be punished by a fine not exceeding twice the amount claimed or imprisonment of two (2) years, or both, at the discretion of the court.
explanation: Claim fraud is unlawful. It includes both presenting a fraudulent claim and preparing or signing a fraudulent document intended to support a claim. Do not confuse a claim that is honestly disputed or imperfectly documented with a knowingly fraudulent claim; the statutory elements matter.

verbatim: Any person having any claim upon the policy issued pursuant to this chapter shall, without any unnecessary delay, present to the insurance company concerned a written notice of claim setting forth the nature, extent and duration of the injuries sustained as certified by a duly licensed physician. Notice of claim must be filed within six (6) months from the date of accident, otherwise, the claim shall be deemed waived. Action or suit for recovery of damage due to loss or injury must be brought, in proper cases, with the Commissioner or the courts within one (1) year from denial of the claim, otherwise, the claimant’s right of action shall prescribe.
explanation: This is a special deadline for claims under the compulsory motor-vehicle insurance chapter: written notice within six months of the accident, then an action within one year from denial of claim. Do not automatically apply these deadlines to every ordinary life, fire, or health policy.

sourceRefs.section: c. Prescription of action and jurisdiction (Sections 63, 397, 439; Civil Code Article 1144)

verbatim: The Commissioner shall have the power to adjudicate claims and complaints involving any loss, damage or liability for which an insurer may be answerable under any kind of policy or contract of insurance, or for which such insurer may be liable under a contract of suretyship, or for which a reinsurer may be sued under any contract of reinsurance it may have entered into; or for which a mutual benefit association may be held liable under the membership certificates it has issued to its members, where the amount of any such loss, damage or liability, excluding interest, cost and attorney’s fees, being claimed or sued upon any kind of insurance, bond, reinsurance contract, or membership certificate does not exceed in any single claim Five million pesos (₱5,000,000.00). The power of the Commissioner does not cover the relationship between the insurance company and its agents/brokers but is limited to adjudicating claims and complaints filed by the insured against the insurance company. The authority to adjudicate granted to the Commissioner under this section shall be concurrent with that of the civil courts, but the filing of a complaint with the Commissioner shall preclude the civil courts from taking cognizance of a suit involving the same subject matter.
explanation: This section addresses which insurance disputes the Insurance Commissioner may adjudicate and states a ₱5 million threshold in the text of R.A. No. 10607, excluding interest, costs, and attorney’s fees. It is not itself a general deadline for filing a case. Check later laws and current Commission rules before relying on the threshold in a live dispute.

sourceRefs.section: c. Prescription of action and jurisdiction (Sections 63, 397, 439; Civil Code Article 1144)

verbatim: The following actions must be brought within ten years from the time the right of action accrues: (1) Upon a written contract; (2) Upon an obligation created by law; (3) Upon a judgment.
explanation: Article 1144 sets a general ten-year period for the listed categories, but do not automatically use it for every insurance dispute. A special provision of the Insurance Code or a valid policy limitation clause—subject to Section 63 and applicable jurisprudence—may govern. Identify exactly what action is being filed and when the cause of action accrued.

sourceRefs.section: c. Prescription of action and jurisdiction (Sections 63, 397, 439; Civil Code Article 1144)

verbatim: The creditor is not bound to accept payment or performance by a third person who has no interest in the fulfillment of the obligation, unless there is a stipulation to the contrary. Whoever pays for another may demand from the debtor what he has paid, except that if he paid without the knowledge or against the will of the debtor, he can recover only insofar as the payment has been beneficial to the debtor.
explanation: Article 1236 generally addresses when a third person can pay someone else’s debt and recover from the debtor. It is not the principal insurance-subrogation provision, but it can help distinguish ordinary reimbursement after payment from the insurer’s statutory/equitable rights after indemnifying an insured loss.

verbatim: If the plaintiff’s property has been insured, and he has received indemnity from the insurance company for the injury or loss arising out of the wrong or breach of contract complained of, the insurance company shall be subrogated to the rights of the insured against the wrongdoer or the person who has violated the contract. If the amount paid by the insurance company does not fully cover the injury or loss, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to recover the deficiency from the person causing the loss or injury.
explanation: Once the insurer indemnifies the insured for property loss caused by another’s wrong or breach, the insurer steps into the insured’s shoes to pursue the wrongdoer up to the amount paid. If the insurance payment does not cover the entire loss, the insured may pursue the remaining deficiency, subject to rules against double recovery.

The NPC is attached to the DICT and headed by a Privacy Commissioner (also Chairman), assisted by two Deputy Privacy Commissioners for Data Processing Systems and for Policies and Planning. All are appointed by the President for three-year terms, reappointable for another three years. The Commissioner must be at least 35, of good moral character, unquestionable integrity and known probity, and a recognized IT and data-privacy expert (Secretary rank); Deputies must be recognized ICT and data-privacy experts (Undersecretary rank).

The Commission may establish its own Secretariat with administrative, technical and support services; members are appointed under Civil Service Law. A majority must have served at least five years in a government agency involved in processing personal information (e.g. SSS, GSIS, LTO, BIR, PhilHealth, COMELEC, DFA, DOJ, PhilPost).

NPC functions (a)-(q): ensure PIC compliance; receive complaints, investigate, facilitate ADR settlement, adjudicate, award indemnity and publicize reports (as a collegial body except on amicable settlement); issue cease-and-desist orders and processing bans for national-security/public-interest detriment; compel compliance; monitor government security measures; coordinate policy; publish guides and filing-system directories; recommend prosecution and Sec. 25-29 penalties to the DOJ; review privacy codes; assist and advise; interpret the Act; propose legislation; and coordinate cross-border enforcement.

Key definitions: (f) Information and Communications System (system plus procedures for electronic data); (g) Personal Information (identifies alone or in combination, tangible or not); (h) Personal Information Controller (controls or directs processing; excludes mere instructed performers and personal/family/household activity); (i) Personal Information Processor (qualified outsourced processor); (j) Processing (any lifecycle operation); (k) Privileged Information (privileged under Rules of Court and other laws); (l) Sensitive Personal Information (four statutory categories).

Broad scope: all personal-information types and any involved natural or juridical person, including offshore controllers/processors using Philippine equipment or maintaining a local office/branch/agency (subject to Sec. 5). Exclusions (a)-(g): government position/contract-service/benefit information; journalistic, artistic, literary or research processing; public-authority functions; bank CISA/AMLA compliance information; and foreign-resident data collected under foreign law.

Nothing in the Act amends or repeals RA 53 protection for publishers, editors and duly accredited reporters of general-circulation publications against compelled disclosure of confidential news sources. Not a blanket media exemption.

Extraterritorial application to foreign acts or practices where (a) processing relates to a Philippine citizen or resident, (b) the entity has a Philippine link (processing here; or abroad about citizens/residents with links such as a Philippine contract, central management and control, or a local branch/agency/office/subsidiary whose parent or affiliate accesses the data), and (c) other links such as carrying on business here or collecting/holding data through a Philippine entity.

Cumulative principles of transparency, legitimate purpose and proportionality. Data must be collected for specified, legitimate, declared purposes and compatibly processed; processed fairly and lawfully; accurate, relevant and updated; adequate and not excessive; retained only as necessary; and kept identifiable no longer than necessary (longer historical/statistical/scientific storage only as laid down in law with safeguards). The PIC must implement these principles.

Lawful processing requires no legal prohibition plus at least one basis: (a) consent; (b) contract necessity or requested pre-contract steps; (c) legal-obligation compliance; (d) vital interests including life and health; (e) national emergency, public order and safety, or public-authority functions; or (f) legitimate interests of the PIC or disclosing third party unless overridden by constitutional fundamental rights. Consent is one basis, not the only one.

Default prohibition on processing sensitive and privileged information, except: (a) specific prior consent (all parties for privileged exchanges); (b) existing laws/regulations guaranteeing protection without requiring consent; (c) life-and-health necessity where consent is inexpressible; (d) lawful noncommercial public-organization objectives with statutory safeguards; (e) medical treatment by qualified providers with adequate protection; or (f) legal proceedings, claims, or government/public-authority provision.

A PIC may subcontract processing but stays responsible for safeguards: confidentiality, prevention of unauthorized use, and general legal compliance. The PIP must also comply with the Act and applicable laws.

PICs may invoke privileged communication over privileged information they lawfully control or process; evidence gathered on privileged information is inadmissible subject to existing laws and regulations. Privilege must first exist under another law; Sec. 15 creates none for ordinary data.

Data-subject rights: (a) be informed of processing; (b) be furnished processing details and PIC identity; (c) reasonable access on demand to contents, sources, recipients, manner, reasons, automated processes, dates, and PIC designation; (d) dispute and obtain immediate correction of inaccuracies (unless vexatious/unreasonable), with propagation to recipients; (e) suspend, withdraw or order blocking/removal/destruction on substantial proof of defect, unlawfulness or obsolescence; and (f) indemnification for resulting damages.
Lawful heirs and assigns may invoke the data subject's Sec. 16 rights after death or upon incapacity or inability to exercise them.

Where data is processed electronically in a structured, commonly used format, the data subject may obtain a reusable electronic or structured copy of data undergoing processing. The Commission may specify formats, standards, modalities and transfer procedures. Separate from the Sec. 16 list.

Secs. 16-18 do not apply to research-only scientific/statistical use with no actions or decisions regarding the subject, strict confidentiality and purpose limitation; nor to processing gathered for criminal, administrative or tax-liability investigations.

The PIC must implement reasonable, proportionate organizational, physical and technical measures against unlawful or accidental destruction, alteration, disclosure and processing — covering natural and human dangers, calibrated to data sensitivity, risk, size, best practices and cost. Required components: network safeguards, security policy, vulnerability process, and monitoring with breach response. Third-party processors must implement the same measures; personnel stay bound by confidentiality after service ends. Sec. 20(f): prompt NPC and subject notification on reasonably believed unauthorized acquisition of SPI or identity-fraud-enabling data with likely real risk of serious harm, with prescribed content and limited delay.

The PIC is accountable for Act compliance and must use contractual or other reasonable means to secure comparable protection during third-party processing. The PIC must designate accountable individual(s) and disclose their identity to any data subject on request.

Government-held SPI must be secured, as far as practicable, with the most appropriate ICT-industry standard as recommended by the Commission. Each agency or instrumentality head is responsible for compliance; the Commission monitors and may recommend action toward minimum standards.

On-site/online access to government SPI requires source-agency-head security clearance (except under Commission guidelines). Off-site transport or access requires a submitted request with agency-head approval within two business days (inaction is disapproval), capped at 1,000 records at a time and using the Commission-recognized most secure encryption standard.

Government contracts potentially involving SPI of 1,000 or more individuals oblige the agency to require the contractor and its employees to register their processing system with the Commission and comply with the Act, including Sec. 23, as agencies and employees do.
Unauthorized processing: PI draws 1-3 years and P500,000-P2,000,000; SPI draws 3-6 years and P500,000-P4,000,000.
Unauthorized access due to negligence: PI draws 1-3 years and P500,000-P2,000,000; SPI draws 3-6 years and P500,000-P4,000,000.
Knowing or negligent improper disposal in publicly accessible areas or trash: PI draws 6 months-2 years and P100,000-P500,000; SPI draws 1-3 years and P100,000-P1,000,000.
Processing for purposes unauthorized by the subject, the Act or existing law: PI draws 1 year 6 months-5 years and P500,000-P1,000,000; SPI draws 2-7 years and P500,000-P2,000,000.
Knowing, unlawful system intrusion where PI or SPI is stored: 1-3 years and P500,000-P2,000,000.
A PIC that, knowing of a breach and the Sec. 20(f) duty, intentionally or by omission conceals it or its extent: 1 year 6 months-5 years and P500,000-P1,000,000.
Malicious disclosure: a PIC, PIP or their officials/employees/agents who with malice or bad faith disclose unwarranted or false PI/SPI they obtained: 1 year 6 months-5 years and P500,000-P1,000,000.
Unauthorized disclosure to a third party without consent, outside Sec. 31: PI draws 1-3 years and P500,000-P1,000,000; SPI draws 3-5 years and P500,000-P2,000,000.
A combination or series of Secs. 25-32 acts: 3-6 years and P1,000,000-P5,000,000.

For juridical-person offenders, participating or grossly negligent responsible officers are penalized, and the court may suspend or revoke Act rights. Aliens are deported after serving the penalty. Public officers/employees guilty under Secs. 27-28 may suffer disqualification.
Large-scale: the maximum of the respective scale applies where PI of at least 100 persons is harmed, affected or involved.
Public-officer offenders acting in the exercise of duties suffer accessory disqualification from public office for double the criminal penalty's term.
Restitution for aggrieved parties is governed by the New Civil Code.
A mark is any visible sign capable of distinguishing an enterprise's goods (trademark) or services (service mark), including a stamped or marked container of goods.
Rights in a mark are acquired through registration validly made under the law.

Bars to registration: (a) immoral, deceptive, scandalous or disparaging matter; (b) Philippine or foreign flags, arms or insignia; (c) living-individual identifiers (or a deceased President's widow) without consent; (d) identity with registered or earlier-filed marks for same, related or confusingly similar goods/services; (e)-(f) well-known marks and their translations; (g) misleading marks; (h)-(j) generic, customary or descriptive matter; (k) functional shapes; (l) color alone undefined by form; (m) public-order or morality violations.

The Filipino-or-English application must state the registration request, applicant identity and nationality/domicile/establishment, organizing law, agent, priority and color claims, three-dimensional status, reproductions, transliteration/translation, Nice-classed goods/services, and signature or self-identification.
After the opposition period lapses or opposition is denied, the Office issues the certificate of registration on fee payment, with notice published in the IPO Gazette.
The certificate is prima facie (rebuttable) evidence of registration validity, registrant ownership, and the exclusive right to use the mark for the specified and related goods/services.

Ten-year duration, conditioned on filing a declaration of actual use with evidence (or valid obstacle-based reasons) within one year from the fifth anniversary; otherwise the mark is removed from the Register.
Renewal for successive ten-year periods on fee payment and request filed within six months before expiration, or within six months after on payment of the additional fee.

A person believing he is or will be damaged may petition for cancellation within five years from registration; anytime cancellation lies for genericness, abandonment, fraud or contrariety to the Act, source misrepresentation, or three-plus years of uninterrupted non-use without legitimate reason. The section also allocates jurisdiction over enforcement and cancellation actions.

Non-use is excused only by circumstances independent of the owner's will; lack of funds never excuses. Non-distinctiveness-altering use, class-spanning use, and qualifying related-company or controlled-user use are preserved under the stated conditions.

The registered owner may prevent unauthorized commercial use of identical or similar signs or containers for identical or similar goods/services where confusion is likely; identical signs on identical goods/services presume confusion. Registered well-known marks extend to dissimilar goods/services where use indicates a connection and owner interests are likely damaged.

Infringing conduct: (155.1) unauthorized commercial use of a reproduction, counterfeit, copy or colorable imitation of a registered mark, container or dominant feature in connection with sale, offering, distribution or advertising (including preparatory steps) where confusion, mistake or deception is likely; or (155.2) reproducing or imitating the mark or dominant feature and applying it to commercial labels, packaging or advertising where confusion is likely. Either act infringes regardless of actual sale.

Remedies: damages measured by complainant's lost profit, defendant's actual profit, or a reasonable percentage of gross sales or service value; impounding of sales records during suit; doubling on shown actual intent to mislead or defraud; and injunction on proper showing.

Publicly identified goodwill in goods, business or services is a property right with or without a registered mark. Unfair competition is passing off through deception or bad-faith means, or acts calculated to that result. Deemed acts: confusing general appearance of goods; artifice implying another's services; and false or bad-faith discrediting statements. Secs. 156, 157 and 161 remedies apply mutatis mutandis.

D-01: the syllabus cites this provision under Trade Name, but it defines collective mark - a visible sign designated as such in the application, capable of distinguishing the origin or other common characteristic (including quality) of different enterprises' goods or services used under the registered owner's control. The actual trade-name definition is Sec. 121.3; verify against RA 8293.
A trade name is the name or designation identifying or distinguishing an enterprise - the enterprise itself, not a particular product.

A name or designation contrary to public order or morals, particularly one liable to deceive trade circles or the public about the nature of the identified enterprise, may not be used as a trade name.

Trade names are protected even before or without registration; confusing subsequent use as a trade name, mark or collective mark is unlawful. Secs. 153-156 and 166-167 remedies apply mutatis mutandis. Ownership transfers only with the enterprise or relevant part, with Secs. 149.2-149.4 applying mutatis mutandis.
A technical solution of a problem in any field that is new, involves an inventive step and is industrially applicable is patentable, whether a product, process or improvement.

Excluded subject matter: (22.1) discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods; (22.2) mental-act, game or business schemes and computer programs; (22.3) surgical, therapeutic and diagnostic methods (not their products); (22.4) plant varieties, animal breeds, essentially biological processes (not micro-organisms or microbiological processes); (22.5) aesthetic creations; (22.6) public-order or morality violations.
Utility models require novelty and industrial applicability; Sec. 21 applies except for inventive step, which is not a condition.

An industrial design is any composition of lines or colors or three-dimensional form giving a special appearance to and serving as pattern for an industrial product or handicraft - appearance, not function.
Only new or original designs are protected; purely technical or functional shapes and designs contrary to public order, health or morals are excluded.
An invention forming part of prior art is not new.

Prior art is everything publicly available worldwide before the filing or priority date, plus the contents of qualifying earlier-filed published Philippine patent, utility-model or design applications, subject to the section's conditions.
Twelve-month grace: pre-filing disclosures by the inventor, by a patent office in specified circumstances, or by third parties deriving from the inventor do not prejudice novelty.
An invention involves an inventive step if, given prior art, it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art at the filing or priority date.
An invention producible and usable in any industry is industrially applicable.
The patent right belongs to the inventor, heirs or assigns; joint makers own jointly.
First-to-file: among independent makers of the same invention, the right belongs to the filer with the earliest filing or priority date.

Commissioned inventions belong to the commissioner absent contrary contract. Employee inventions belong to the employee where inventive activity is outside regular duties (even with employer resources), and to the employer where they result from regularly assigned duties, absent contrary agreement.

Reciprocity-based priority: a local application expressly claiming priority, filed within twelve months of the foreign filing, with a certified foreign copy and English translation within six months of Philippine filing, is treated as filed on the foreign date.

One adjudged owner of the patent right may, within three months after finality, prosecute the application, file anew, request refusal, or seek cancellation. One adjudged the true inventor may be substituted as patentee or elect cancellation, with damages if warranted.

The Filipino-or-English application contains the grant request, description, necessary drawings, claims and abstract; no patent issues without inventor identification. Claims define the protection scope.
The filing date is the Office's receipt date of at least an express or implied Philippine-patent request, applicant identification, and a Filipino-or-English description with claims.
Compliant, fee-paid applications are granted, effective on IPO Gazette publication of the grant. Final examiner refusals are appealable to the Director under the Act and Regulations.
Patent term: twenty years from the application filing date.
Interested persons may seek full or partial cancellation for non-patentability, insufficient enabling disclosure, or public-order/morality contrariety.

Utility models expire without renewal seven years after filing. Cancellation lies for disqualification, registration-requirement failure, insufficient description or claims, missing drawings, or non-inventor ownership.

Industrial designs run five years from filing, renewable for at most two consecutive five-year periods. Cancellation lies for non-registrability, lack of novelty, or added subject matter, in full or in part.

Product patents exclude unauthorized making, using, offering, selling or importing; process patents exclude unauthorized process use and dealings in directly or indirectly obtained products. Owners may assign, transmit by succession, and license.
First sale/exhaustion: use of a patented product put on the Philippine market by or with the owner's express consent is beyond the owner's control after that marketing.
Further limits: qualifying private non-commercial acts, experimental acts, individual-case medicine preparation, and use aboard specified temporarily or accidentally present foreign conveyances.
Good-faith prior users (or serious preparers) before the filing or priority date may continue enterprise use within the patent territory; the right transfers only with the enterprise or business.

Government agencies or authorized third persons may exploit the invention without agreement for public-interest grounds (national security, nutrition, health, vital sectors) or adjudged anti-competitive exploitation, subject to Secs. 95-97 and 100-102 conditions.
All technology transfer arrangements must comply with the Chapter, whose policy is encouraging technology transfer while preventing or controlling IP abuses harming competition and trade.
Absent contrary agreement, licensing does not prevent the licensor from further licensing or self-exploitation.
The licensee may exploit the arrangement's subject matter during the whole arrangement term.

The Director of Legal Affairs may compulsorily license a capable exploiter on grounds including national emergency or extreme urgency, vital public interests, or adjudged anti-competitive exploitation.

Compulsory-license safeguards: purpose-limited scope and duration; non-exclusive; non-assignable except with the enterprise or goodwill; predominantly for the Philippine market (anti-competitive exception); termination when grounds cease and are unlikely to recur; and adequate patentee remuneration.
Patents and applications are assignable, inheritable, bequeathable and licensable; the written instrument must be recorded in the Office and is ineffective against third parties until recorded.

Unauthorized product or process acts constitute infringement. Civil relief: damages, attorney's fees, expenses, injunction; reasonable royalty where damages are unascertainable; up to triple damages; removal or destruction of infringing articles; and contributory liability for active inducement or knowing supply of specially adapted components.

Repetition of infringement after final judgment, by the infringer or connivers, is criminal: 6 months-3 years and/or P100,000-P300,000, without prejudice to civil damages. The action prescribes in three years from commission.

Literary and artistic works are original intellectual creations protected from creation: books and writings; periodicals; oral-delivery works; letters; dramatic, musical and choreographic works; art and applied art; maps, plans and technical works; photographs; audiovisual works; illustrations and ads; computer programs; and other literary, scholarly, scientific and artistic works - irrespective of expression mode, content, quality or purpose.

Exclusive economic rights, subject to Chapter VIII: reproduction; transformation (dramatization, translation, adaptation, abridgment, arrangement); first public distribution; rental of specified work types; public display; public performance; and other communication to the public.
Copyright vests automatically on creation, irrespective of expression mode, content, quality or purpose; deposit and notice are not conditions.

Derivative works (alterations of literary/artistic works; original collections and compilations) are protected as new works without affecting subsisting original-work copyright or implying use rights. Publishers hold only the typographical-arrangement reproduction right in the published edition.

No protection for ideas, procedures, systems, methods, concepts, principles, discoveries or mere data as such (even as embodied); day-to-day news and mere press items; or official legislative, administrative or legal texts and their official translations. Expression, not idea, is protected.

No copyright subsists in Philippine Government works, but commercial exploitation needs prior creating-agency approval and may incur royalties. GOCC works are separately registrable by the corporation. The Government may receive and hold transferred copyrights.
The author is the natural person who created the work; ownership may follow special employee, commissioned, joint and audiovisual rules.

Ownership: original works belong to the author; joint authors co-own (separable parts to their authors); employee creations outside regular duties belong to the employee, those from assigned duties to the employer absent agreement; commissioned works belong to the commissioner but copyright stays with the creator absent written stipulation otherwise; audiovisual copyright is shared per statute subject to producer exercise rights; letters belong to the writer under Civil Code Art. 723.

Publishers presumptively represent published authors and may sue for infringement. Anonymous and pseudonymous works run fifty years from first lawful publication; revealed identity invokes Sec. 213.1.

Terms: ordinary works life plus 50 years (posthumous included); joint works last-survivor life plus 50; anonymous/pseudonymous 50 years from first lawful publication (unpublished 50 from making); applied art 25 from making; photographic/audiovisual 50 from publication or making. Post-death/post-publication terms begin January 1 of the next year.
Copyright or exclusive-right owners may deposit two copies with the National Library (and law works with the Supreme Court Library) for record completion; deposit is not a protection condition.
Published or for-sale copies may bear a notice naming the owner and the first-publication year (plus death year for posthumous copies). Notice identifies; it does not create copyright.

Copyright is assignable or licensable in whole or part, with inter vivos transfers indicated in writing and exclusive licensees receiving in-scope rights and remedies; copyright is distinct from the material object; owners may transfer under the Act; and collective-management societies need IPO accreditation to enforce member rights.

Non-infringing acts (a)-(l): private free recitation/performance and qualifying charitable/religious use; justified attributed quotations; unreserved media use of lectures and current topics; current-events reporting; attributed teaching illustration; limited educational broadcast recordings; broadcasters' ephemeral recordings; qualifying public-interest institutional uses; nonprofit no-fee performances; specified public display; judicial/legal-advice use; and nonprofit specialized-format copies for the print-disabled. Each is conditional and must not conflict with normal exploitation or unreasonably prejudice legitimate interests.

Fair use for criticism, comment, news, teaching (including limited classroom copies), scholarship, research and similar purposes - plus qualifying interoperability decompilation - is not infringement. Four factors: purpose and character; work nature; amount and substantiality; market or value effect. Unpublished status alone does not bar fair use.
Secs. 184 and 186 preserve the Government's right to make or authorize translations, adaptations or publication of a work when necessary to its functions.

A natural person may make one private copy of a published work exclusively for research and private study, excluding building-form architecture, reprographic whole/substantial books and graphic musical works, data compilations, computer programs (except Sec. 189), and exploitation-conflicting reproduction.

Nonprofit libraries and archives may make limited mandate-necessary copies: fragile or rare works; isolated articles or brief research portions; and preservation or replacement of lost, destroyed or unusable publisher-unavailable copies.

Infringement by direct commission; knowing, controllable benefit from another's infringement; or knowing inducement, causation or material contribution. Relief: injunction; actual damages, costs, expenses and profits; statutory damages under the minimum and factors; increased technological-measure/RMI damages; and seizure or impounding of evidence.

Criminal penalties for infringement or aiding it: first offense 1-3 years and P50,000-P150,000; second 3 years 1 day-6 years and P150,000-P500,000; third and later 6 years 1 day-9 years and P500,000-P1,500,000. Maximum applies to specified technological-measure circumvention and RMI violations with knowing distribution, broadcast or communication.

Points of attachment: works (nationality, residence, headquarters, Philippine erection or first/30-day publication); performances (nationality, place, fixed or broadcast inclusion); sound recordings (producer nationality, first publication); and broadcasts (headquarters, transmitter situs).

Moral rights independent of economic rights: attribution; pre-publication alteration or withholding; objection to prejudicial distortion, mutilation, modification or derogatory action; and restraint of false or distorted name use.

No compelled creation or publication (damages for breach); written waiver allowed but never for false attribution or prejudicial name use; collective-work attribution deemed waived unless reserved; necessary publication-related editing is no violation; Sec. 193.1 attribution endures in perpetuity after death while 193.2-193.4 run with economic rights. Moral rights are unassignable and unlicensable.

Performers' exclusive authorization rights over live-performance broadcast and communication, fixation, and fixed-performance reproduction, distribution, rental and making available, plus identification and integrity moral rights - neighboring rights distinct from the underlying work's copyright.

Sound-recording producers' exclusive authorization rights over reproduction, first public distribution, commercial rental and making available, with related remuneration provisions - protecting the recording, not necessarily the underlying work.

Broadcasting organizations' exclusive rights over rebroadcasting, recording for public television communication, and fresh-transmission use of records - signal rights, not automatic rights in underlying works.
Chapter VIII copyright limitations apply mutatis mutandis to performers, sound-recording producers and broadcasting organizations.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 82 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim:
ART. 82. Coverage. The provisions of this Title shall apply to employees in all establishments and undertakings whether for profit or not, but not to government employees, managerial employees, field personnel, members of the family of the employer who are dependent on him for support, domestic helpers, persons in the personal service of another, and workers who are paid by results as determined by the Secretary of Labor in appropriate regulations.

As used herein, "managerial employees" refer to those whose primary duty consists of the management of the establishment in which they are employed or of a department or subdivision thereof, and to other officers or members of the managerial staff.

"Field personnel" shall refer to non-agricultural employees who regularly perform their duties away from the principal place of business or branch office of the employer and whose actual hours of work in the field cannot be determined with reasonable certainty.
explanation: Art. 82 is the gatekeeper of Title I (Arts. 82-96: hours, rest days, holidays, SIL, service charges). Everyone is covered EXCEPT the seven listed groups — memorize them as a closed list. Two definitions do the heavy lifting: 'managerial employees' (primary duty = management, plus officers/members of managerial staff — Penaranda shows a supervisor can be managerial STAFF even if not a managerial employee) and 'field personnel' (two cumulative tests: away from principal/branch office AND hours not determinable with reasonable certainty). Payroll angle: misclassifying a covered worker as exempt wipes out OT, holiday, and SIL liabilities on paper — exactly what David and Auto Bus punish. Remember: 'paid by results' is NOT a blanket exemption — the IRR (Rules I, IV, V) qualifies it, and task/commission workers get holiday and SIL pay unless they are field personnel.

citation: Omnibus Rules, Book III, Rule I, Sec. 2
verbatim:
SECTION 2. Exemption. — The provisions of this Rule shall not apply to the following persons if they qualify for exemption under the conditions set forth herein:

(a) Government employees whether employed by the National Government or any of its political subdivision, including those employed in government-owned and/or controlled corporations;

(b) Managerial employees, if they meet all of the following conditions: (1) Their primary duty consists of the management of the establishment in which they are employed or of a department or sub-division thereof. (2) They customarily and regularly direct the work of two or more employees therein. (3) They have the authority to hire or fire employees of lower rank; or their suggestions and recommendations as to hiring and firing and as to the promotion or any other change of status of other employees, are given particular weight.

(c) Officers or members of a managerial staff if they perform the following duties and responsibilities: (1) The primary duty consists of the performance of work directly related to management policies of their employer; (2) Customarily and regularly exercise discretion and independent judgment; and (3) (i) Regularly and directly assist a proprietor or a managerial employee whose primary duty consists of the management of the establishment in which he is employed or subdivision thereof; or (ii) execute under general supervision work along specialized or technical lines requiring special training, experience, or knowledge; or (iii) execute, under general supervision, special assignments and tasks; and (4) Who do not devote more than 20 percent of their hours worked in a work week to activities which are not directly and closely related to the performance of the work described in paragraphs (1), (2) and (3) above.

(d) Domestic servants and persons in the personal service of another if they perform such services in the employer's home which are usually necessary or desirable for the maintenance and enjoyment thereof, or minister to the personal comfort, convenience, or safety of the employer as well as the members of his employer's household.

(e) Workers who are paid by results, including those who are paid on piece-work, "takay," "pakiao" or task basis, and other non-time work if their output rates are in accordance with the standards prescribed under Section 8, Rule VII, Book Three of these regulations, or where such rates have been fixed by the Secretary of Labor and Employment in accordance with the aforesaid Section.

(f) Non-agricultural field personnel if they regularly perform their duties away from the principal or branch office or place of business of the employer and whose actual hours of work in the field cannot be determined with reasonable certainty.
explanation: This is the regulation Art. 82 points to ('as determined by the Secretary of Labor'). Exam focus: the THREE-part managerial-employee test (manage + direct 2+ employees + hire/fire authority or weighted recommendations) versus the FOUR-part managerial-STAFF test (management-related work + discretion and independent judgment + assist-a-manager/specialized-work/special-assignments + the 20% cap on unrelated work). Penaranda failed the first test but met the second — and either one takes the worker out of Title I. Practical application: job titles prove nothing; DOLE and the courts test actual duties (David's butcher, Auto Bus's driver). For 'paid by results' (e), the exemption is conditional on proper output rates — it never excuses minimum-wage violations (see Art. 124 last paragraphs).

citation: Labor Code, Art. 83 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim:
ART. 83. Normal Hours of Work. The normal hours of work of any employee shall not exceed eight (8) hours a day.

Health personnel in cities and municipalities with a population of at least one million (1,000,000) or in hospitals and clinics with a bed capacity of at least one hundred (100) shall hold regular office hours for eight (8) hours a day, for five (5) days a week, exclusive of time for meals, except where the exigencies of the service require that such personnel work for six (6) days or forty-eight (48) hours, in which case, they shall be entitled to an additional compensation of at least thirty percent (30%) of their regular wage for work on the sixth day. For purposes of this Article, "health personnel" shall include resident physicians, nurses, nutritionists, dietitians, pharmacists, social workers, laboratory technicians, paramedical technicians, psychologists, midwives, attendants and all other hospital or clinic personnel.
explanation: The 8-hour day is the anchor of all premium computations (OT, night differential, holiday pay). Anything beyond 8 hours is overtime by definition — UNLESS a valid compressed workweek (CWW) redefines the normal day. The second paragraph is a special 40-hour week (5 days x 8 hours, meals excluded) for health personnel in big cities (1M+ population) or big facilities (100+ beds); exigency sixth-day work earns at least +30%. Compliance note: government health workers are Title I-exempt and fall under RA 7305 instead (DOLE edition footnote). Remember: 'exclusive of time for meals' — the 60-minute meal break sits outside the 8 hours.

citation: DOLE Dept. Advisory No. 02, Series of 2004 (Compressed Workweek Schemes)
verbatim:
For purposes of this Advisory, a CWW scheme is an alternative arrangement whereby the normal workweek is reduced to less than six days but the total number of normal work hours per week shall remain at 48 hours. The normal workday is increased to more than eight hours without corresponding overtime premium. This concept can be adjusted accordingly in cases where the normal workweek of the firm is five days.

[...] DOLE shall recognize CWW schemes adopted in accordance with the following: 1. The CWW scheme is undertaken as a result of an express and voluntary agreement of majority of the covered employees or their duly authorized representatives. This agreement may be expressed through collective bargaining or other legitimate workplace mechanisms of participation such as labor-management councils, employee assemblies or referenda. 2. In firms using substances, chemicals and processes or operating under conditions where there are airborne contaminants, human carcinogens or noise prolonged exposure to which may pose hazards to the employees' health and safety, there must be a certification from an accredited health and safety organization or practitioner or from the firm's safety committee that work beyond eight hours is within threshold limits or tolerable levels of exposure, as set in the OSHS. 3. The employer shall notify DOLE, through the Regional Office having jurisdiction over the workplace, of the adoption of the CWW scheme. [...]

A CWW scheme which complies with the foregoing conditions shall have the following effects: 1. Unless there is a more favorable practice existing in the firm, work beyond eight hours will not be compensable by overtime premium provided the total number of hours worked per day shall not exceed twelve (12) hours. In any case, any work performed beyond 12 hours a day or 48 hours a week shall be subject to overtime premium. 2. Consistent with Article 85 of the Labor Code, employees under a CWW scheme are entitled to meal periods of not less than sixty (60) minutes. [...] 3. Adoption of the CWW scheme shall in no case result in diminution of existing benefits. Reversion to the normal eight-hour workday shall not constitute a diminution of benefits.
explanation: CWW is the syllabus's 'But see' under normal hours — the lawful way to schedule 10- or 12-hour days without OT premium. Three conditions (majority voluntary agreement + OSHS certification where hazardous + DOLE notice) and three effects (no OT premium up to 12 hours/day; 60-minute meals intact; no diminution — and reverting to 8 hours is NOT diminution). Two hard ceilings survive: work past 12 hours a day or 48 hours a week ALWAYS earns OT premium. Payroll application: a 4x12 schedule pays straight time for all 48 hours; a 13th hour in a day reverts to Art. 87 rates. Remember: without proof of voluntary agreement, the employer owes OT 'as if the CWW scheme did not exist.' Excluded workplaces: construction, health services, heavy manual labor, OSHS-exceeding exposures. The broader flexible-work advisories (DA 02-2009, DA 04-2010) could not be retrieved — cited by title only in the lesson.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 84 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim:
ART. 84. Hours Worked. Hours worked shall include (a) all time during which an employee is required to be on duty or to be at a prescribed workplace; and (b) all time during which an employee is suffered or permitted to work.

Rest periods of short duration during working hours shall be counted as hours worked.
explanation: Two alternative tests: (a) required presence (on duty or at a prescribed place) or (b) suffered/permitted work (the employer knew or should have known and let it happen). Either one makes time compensable. 'Suffered or permitted' is the trap: unauthorized-but-known overtime still counts — the remedy is discipline, not non-payment. Short rest periods (Rule I Sec. 7: 5-to-20-minute coffee breaks) are compensable by statute; the 60-minute meal is not. Practical application: payroll controls should capture required early log-ins, through-lunch work, and post-shift completion (Rule I Sec. 4(c)) — all are hours worked if the supervisor knew.

citation: Omnibus Rules, Book III, Rule I, Secs. 3-7
verbatim:
SECTION 3. Hours worked. — The following shall be considered as compensable hours worked: (a) All time during which an employee is required to be on duty or to be at the employer's premises or to be at a prescribed work place; and (b) All time during which an employee is suffered or permitted to work.

SECTION 4. Principles in determining hours worked. — The following general principles shall govern in determining whether the time spent by an employee is considered hours worked for purposes of this Rule: (a) All hours are hours worked which the employee is required to give his employer, regardless of whether or not such hours are spent in productive labor or involve physical or mental exertion. (b) An employee need not leave the premises of the work place in order that his rest period shall not be counted, it being enough that he stops working, may rest completely and may leave his work place, to go elsewhere, whether within or outside the premises of his work place. (c) If the work performed was necessary, or it benefited the employer, or the employee could not abandon his work at the end of his normal working hours because he had no replacement, all time spent for such work shall be considered as hours worked, if the work was with the knowledge of his employer or immediate supervisor. (d) The time during which an employee is inactive by reason of interruptions in his work beyond his control shall be considered working time either if the imminence of the resumption of work requires the employee's presence at the place of work or if the interval is too brief to be utilized effectively and gainfully in the employee's own interest.

SECTION 5. Waiting time. — (a) Waiting time spent by an employee shall be considered as working time if waiting is an integral part of his work or the employee is required or engaged by the employer to wait. (b) An employee who is required to remain on call in the employer's premises or so close thereto that he cannot use the time effectively and gainfully for his own purpose shall be considered as working while on call. An employee who is not required to leave word at his home or with company officials where he may be reached is not working while on call.

SECTION 6. Lectures, meetings, training programs. — Attendance at lectures, meetings, training programs, and other similar activities shall not be counted as working time if all of the following conditions are met: (a) Attendance is outside of the employee's regular working hours; (b) Attendance is in fact voluntary; and (c) The employee does not perform any productive work during such attendance.

SECTION 7. Meal and Rest Periods. — Every employer shall give his employees, regardless of sex, not less than one (1) hour time-off for regular meals, except in the following cases when a meal period of not less than twenty (20) minutes may be given by the employer provided that such shorter meal period is credited as compensable hours worked of the employee: (a) Where the work is non-manual work in nature or does not involve strenuous physical exertion; (b) Where the establishment regularly operates not less than sixteen (16) hours a day; (c) In case of actual or impending emergencies or there is urgent work to be performed on machineries, equipment or installations to avoid serious loss which the employer would otherwise suffer; and (d) Where the work is necessary to prevent serious loss of perishable goods. Rest periods or coffee breaks running from five (5) to twenty (20) minutes shall be considered as compensable working time.
explanation: This is the rule behind nearly every syllabus item on compensable vs non-compensable time. Sec. 4(a): required hours count even if idle (covers power interruptions and idle time together with 4(d): interruption time counts IF presence is required for imminent resumption OR the interval is too brief to use gainfully — if the worker is sent home and free, it does not). Sec. 4(b): a real rest break (stop work, rest completely, free to leave the work place) is not counted. Sec. 4(c): necessary after-hours work with the supervisor's knowledge counts (overtime by sufferance). Sec. 5: waiting counts when integral to the work or the worker is engaged to wait; on-call counts when confined to/near the premises so time cannot be used gainfully (a pager-at-home arrangement with no leave-word requirement does not). Sec. 6: lectures/meetings/training are excluded ONLY if ALL three concur (outside hours + truly voluntary + no productive work) — fail one and the time counts. Sec. 7: shortened 20-minute meals are allowed in the four listed cases but must be CREDITED as compensable; 5-to-20-minute coffee breaks always count. Travel/commuting: ordinary home-to-work travel is not required presence; travel performed as part of the work (required, employer-directed) falls under Sec. 3(a)/4(a). Remember: the pattern is 'required-or-beneficial + known = compensable.'

citation: Labor Code, Art. 85 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 85. Meal Periods. Subject to such regulations as the Secretary of Labor may prescribe, it shall be the duty of every employer to give his employees not less than sixty (60) minutes time-off for their regular meals.
explanation: The 60-minute meal break is a statutory DUTY of the employer and, as a full hour fully free of work, is the paradigmatic non-compensable period — but it is excluded from the 8 hours only when it is a genuine break (Rule I Sec. 4(b): stop work, rest completely, free to leave the work place). Shortened meals (20+ minutes in the four Rule I Sec. 7 cases) must be credited as compensable hours. Practical application: 'working lunches' at the desk are compensable hours worked, not meal time — a common payroll understatement.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 86 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 86. Night-Shift Differential. Every employee shall be paid a night shift differential of not less than ten percent (10%) of his regular wage for each hour of work performed between ten o'clock in the evening and six o'clock in the morning.
explanation: Night differential (NSD) is at least +10% of the regular wage for EVERY hour worked in the 10 p.m.-6 a.m. window — it attaches per hour, so a 10 p.m.-6 a.m. shift earns 8 hours of NSD. 'Every employee' means Title I-covered employees; it stacks with overtime and holiday premiums (each premium is computed on its own base). Payroll angle: NSD is part of the wage base for 13th-month purposes ONLY if integrated as basic salary by agreement/practice (Revised Guidelines) — otherwise excluded. Remember the window by the mnemonic '10-to-6, plus-10%.'

citation: Labor Code, Art. 87 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 87. Overtime Work. Work may be performed beyond eight (8) hours a day provided that the employee is paid for the overtime work, an additional compensation equivalent to his regular wage plus at least twenty-five percent (25%) thereof. Work performed beyond eight hours on a holiday or rest day shall be paid an additional compensation equivalent to the rate of the first eight hours on a holiday or rest day plus at least thirty percent (30%) thereof.
explanation: Two OT formulas: (1) ordinary day: hourly rate x 125% per OT hour; (2) holiday/rest day: (first-8-hours holiday/rest-day hourly rate) x 130% per OT hour. The second formula compounds — e.g., a regular-holiday rest-day OT hour builds on the 260% base. 'May be performed' signals the general rule that OT requires employee consent; compulsory OT exists only under Art. 89 (and Rule I Sec. 10(f) favorable weather). Practical application: compute the hourly rate from the regular wage (monthly wage x 12 / 365 / 8, or the Rule IV Sec. 2 monthly-paid divisor logic), then apply the premium. Remember: CWW days up to 12 hours are NOT overtime — but any CWW excess reverts to this article.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 88 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 88. Undertime Not Offset by Overtime. Undertime work on any particular day shall not be offset by overtime work on any other day. Permission given to the employee to go on leave on some other day of the week shall not exempt the employer from paying the additional compensation required in this Chapter.
explanation: Each day's OT premium stands alone: Monday's 2-hour undertime cannot cancel Tuesday's 2-hour OT premium, and a mid-week offsetting leave does not erase earned OT pay. This is the anti-averaging rule — weekly-hours averaging (except through a valid CWW) cannot defeat daily OT. Payroll trap: 'flexi-offset' schemes that net undertime against OT within the week violate this article. Remember: undertime affects only the basic wage for that day; overtime always carries its premium.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 89 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim:
ART. 89. Emergency Overtime Work. Any employee may be required by the employer to perform overtime work in any of the following cases: (a) When the country is at war or when any other national or local emergency has been declared by the National Assembly or the Chief Executive; (b) When it is necessary to prevent loss of life or property or in case of imminent danger to public safety due to an actual or impending emergency in the locality caused by serious accidents, fire, flood, typhoon, earthquake, epidemic, or other disaster or calamity; (c) When there is urgent work to be performed on machines, installations, or equipment, in order to avoid serious loss or damage to the employer or some other cause of similar nature; (d) When the work is necessary to prevent loss or damage to perishable goods; and (e) Where the completion or continuation of the work started before the eighth hour is necessary to prevent serious obstruction or prejudice to the business or operations of the employer.

Any employee required to render overtime work under this Article shall be paid the additional compensation required in this Chapter.
explanation: The five closed grounds for COMPULSORY overtime: war/declared emergency; loss-of-life/property or public-safety danger; urgent machine/equipment work; perishable goods; and completion of pre-8th-hour work to prevent serious obstruction or prejudice. 'National Assembly' is stale text for Congress (see DOLE edition footnote). Compulsion never means free work — the last paragraph preserves Art. 87 premiums. Rule I Sec. 10 adds a sixth regulatory ground (favorable weather/environmental conditions) and the clincher: outside these grounds, no employee may be made to work beyond 8 hours against his will. Exam point: refusal of OT is insubordination ONLY within Art. 89/Rule I Sec. 10 grounds.

citation: Omnibus Rules, Book III, Rule I, Secs. 8-10
verbatim:
SECTION 8. Overtime pay. — Any employee covered by this Rule who is permitted or required to work beyond eight (8) hours on ordinary working days shall be paid an additional compensation for the overtime work in the amount equivalent to his regular wage plus at least twenty-five percent (25%) thereof.

SECTION 9. Premium and overtime pay for holiday and rest day work. — (a) Except employees referred to under Section 2 of this Rule, an employee who is permitted or suffered to work on special holidays or on his designated rest days not falling on regular holidays, shall be paid with an additional compensation as premium pay of not less than thirty percent (30%) of his regular wage. For work performed in excess of eight (8) hours on special holidays and rest days not falling on regular holidays, an employee shall be paid an additional compensation for the overtime work equivalent to his rate for the first eight hours on a special holiday or rest day plus at least thirty percent (30%) thereof. (b) Employees of public utility enterprises as well as those employed in non-profit institutions and organizations shall be entitled to the premium and overtime pay provided herein, unless they are specifically excluded from the coverage of this Rule as provided in Section 2 hereof. (c) The payment of additional compensation for work performed on regular holidays shall be governed by Rule IV, Book Three, of these Rules.

SECTION 10. Compulsory overtime work. — In any of the following cases, an employer may require any of his employees to work beyond eight (8) hours a day, provided that the employee required to render overtime work is paid the additional compensation required by these regulations: (a) When the country is at war or when any other national or local emergency has been declared by Congress or the Chief Executive; (b) When overtime work is necessary to prevent loss of life or property, or in case of imminent danger to public safety due to actual or impending emergency in the locality caused by serious accident, fire, floods, typhoons, earthquake, epidemic or other disaster or calamities; (c) When there is urgent work to be performed on machines, installations, or equipment, in order to avoid serious loss or damage to the employer or some other causes of similar nature; (d) When the work is necessary to prevent loss or damage to perishable goods; (e) When the completion or continuation of work started before the 8th hour is necessary to prevent serious obstruction or prejudice to the business or operations of the employer; or (f) When overtime work is necessary to avail of favorable weather or environmental conditions where performance or quality of work is dependent thereon. In cases not falling within any of these enumerated in this Section, no employee may be made to work beyond eight hours a day against his will.
explanation: The payroll-implementation companion to Arts. 87-89. Sec. 8 restates the 125% ordinary-OT rate; Sec. 9(a) gives the rest-day/special-holiday premium (130% for the first 8 hours, then that rate x 130% for OT) and expressly covers public-utility and non-profit employees (Sec. 9(b)) — 'non-profit' is not an exemption. Sec. 10 mirrors Art. 89's five grounds (updating 'National Assembly' to 'Congress') and adds ground (f): favorable weather/environmental conditions — the only compulsory-OT basis found solely in the Rules. The closing sentence is the employee's shield: outside these six grounds, overtime against the worker's will is unlawful. Remember: regular-holiday work rates live in Rule IV, not here (Sec. 9(c)).

citation: Labor Code, Art. 90 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 90. Computation of Additional Compensation. For purposes of computing overtime and other additional remuneration as required by this Chapter, the "regular wage" of an employee shall include the cash wage only, without deduction on account of facilities provided by the employer.
explanation: OT and premium bases use CASH wage only — facilities (meals, lodging) furnished by the employer are neither added to nor deducted from the base. Read with Art. 97(f) (facilities form part of 'wage' for minimum-wage valuation) and Mabeza (facilities deductible from wages only on three conditions): for OT purposes the base stays cash. Practical application: an employee receiving P500/day cash plus P100 meals computes OT on P500, not P600. Remember: 'without deduction' protects the worker both ways — the employer cannot shrink the OT base by the value of facilities.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 91 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim:
ART. 91. Right to Weekly Rest Day. (a) It shall be the duty of every employer, whether operating for profit or not, to provide each of his employees a rest period of not less than twenty-four (24) consecutive hours after every six (6) consecutive normal work days.

(b) The employer shall determine and schedule the weekly rest day of his employees subject to collective bargaining agreement and to such rules and regulations as the Secretary of Labor and Employment may provide. However, the employer shall respect the preference of employees as to their weekly rest day when such preference is based on religious grounds.
explanation: The weekly rest formula: 24 consecutive hours after every 6 consecutive normal work days — the '6+1' rhythm. Scheduling is a management prerogative (employer sets the rest day, CBA and DOLE rules permitting), EXCEPT the employer must respect religious-ground preferences (e.g., Saturday Sabbath, Friday observance). 'Whether operating for profit or not' repeats the Rule I Sec. 9(b) point: non-profits owe rest days too. Practical application: shifting schedules (retail, BPO) must still yield one fixed 24-hour rest in every 7-day cycle; compressing the rest below 24 hours violates (a). Remember: Sunday is NOT the default rest day — it is only special when it is the employee's ESTABLISHED rest day (Art. 93(a)).

citation: Labor Code, Art. 92 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 92. When Employer May Require Work on a Rest Day. The employer may require his employees to work on any day: (a) In case of actual or impending emergencies caused by serious accident, fire, flood, typhoon, earthquake, epidemic or other disaster or calamity to prevent loss of life and property, or imminent danger to public safety; (b) In cases of urgent work to be performed on the machinery, equipment, or installation, to avoid serious loss which the employer would otherwise suffer; (c) In the event of abnormal pressure of work due to special circumstances, where the employer cannot ordinarily be expected to resort to other measures; (d) To prevent loss or damage to perishable goods; (e) Where the nature of the work requires continuous operations and the stoppage of work may result in irreparable injury or loss to the employer; and (f) Under other circumstances analogous or similar to the foregoing as determined by the Secretary of Labor and Employment.
explanation: Six closed grounds for compulsory rest-day work — the rest-day twin of Art. 89, with two distinctive additions: (c) abnormal pressure of work from special circumstances (the classic year-end/seasonal rush ground) and (e) continuous operations where stoppage means irreparable injury or loss (power plants, hospitals, care homes). Outside these grounds, rest-day work needs the employee's consent. Compulsion never cancels premium pay — Art. 93 rates apply to all rest-day work, voluntary or required. Exam point: (f) is a delegation, not a blank check — only the Secretary can declare analogous circumstances.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 93 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim:
ART. 93. Compensation for Rest Day, Sunday or Holiday Work. (a) Where an employee is made or permitted to work on his scheduled rest day, he shall be paid an additional compensation of at least thirty percent (30%) of his regular wage. An employee shall be entitled to such additional compensation for work performed on Sunday only when it is his established rest day.

(b) When the nature of the work of the employee is such that he has no regular workdays and no regular rest days can be scheduled, he shall be paid an additional compensation of at least thirty percent (30%) of his regular wage for work performed on Sundays and holidays.

(c) Work performed on any special holiday shall be paid an additional compensation of at least thirty percent (30%) of the regular wage of the employee. Where such holiday work falls on the employee's scheduled rest day, he shall be entitled to an additional compensation of at least fifty per cent (50%) of his regular wage.

(d) Where the collective bargaining agreement or other applicable employment contract stipulates the payment of a higher premium pay than that prescribed under this Article, the employer shall pay such higher rate.
explanation: The premium-pay ladder: rest-day work = 130%; Sunday work = 130% ONLY if Sunday is the established rest day (syllabus 'Sunday' item — working Sundays on a Tuesday-rest schedule earns no premium); no-fixed-schedule workers = 130% for Sunday AND holiday work; special-holiday work = 130%, rising to 150% when the special holiday falls on the scheduled rest day. Paragraph (d) makes CBA/contract rates a floor-raiser, never a ceiling-lowerer. Cross-check: this text was verified against three hosts (DOLE edition, Lawphil, and the Penaranda footnote quotation). Remember the 150%: it is the ONLY 50%-premium in the Code — special day + rest day coincidence.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 94 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 94. Right to Holiday Pay. (a) Every worker shall be paid his regular daily wage during regular holidays, except in retail and service establishments regularly employing less than ten (10) workers; (b) The employer may require an employee to work on any holiday but such employee shall be paid a compensation equivalent to twice his regular rate; and (c) As used in this Article, "holiday" includes: New Year's Day, Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, the ninth of April, the first of May, the twelfth of June, the fourth of July, the thirtieth of November, the twenty-fifth and thirtieth of December and the day designated by law for holding a general election.
explanation: Holiday pay = 100% of the regular daily wage even when unworked (the great exception to 'no work, no pay'), EXCEPT in retail/service establishments with fewer than 10 workers. Worked regular holidays pay 200% (Rule IV Sec. 4 details the rest-day coincidence: 200% + 30% of 200% = 260%). CRITICAL currency warning: paragraph (c)'s list is INOPERATIVE — it still names July 4th and omits Eidul Fitr/Adha and holiday-economics Monday observance. The current list is EO 292 Sec. 26 AS AMENDED by RA 9492 and RA 9849 (plus RA 10966's December 8 special day). Never quote (c) as the current holiday calendar. David holds pakyaw/task workers entitled to holiday pay unless they are field personnel.

citation: Omnibus Rules, Book III, Rule IV, Secs. 1-5
verbatim:
SECTION 1. Coverage. — This rule shall apply to all employees except: (a) Those of the government and any of the political subdivision, including government-owned and controlled corporation; (b) Those of retail and service establishments regularly employing less than ten (10) workers; (c) Domestic helpers and persons in the personal service of another; (d) Managerial employees as defined in Book Three of the Code; (e) Field personnel and other employees whose time and performance is unsupervised by the employer including those who are engaged on task or contract basis, purely commission basis, or those who are paid a fixed amount for performing work irrespective of the time consumed in the performance thereof.

SECTION 2. Status of employees paid by the month. — Employees who are uniformly paid by the month, irrespective of the number of working days therein, with a salary of not less than the statutory or established minimum wage shall be paid for all days in the month whether worked or not. For this purpose, the monthly minimum wage shall not be less than the statutory minimum wage multiplied by 365 days divided by twelve.

SECTION 3. Holiday Pay. — Every employer shall pay his employees their regular daily wage for any worked regular holidays. As used in the rule, the term 'regular holiday' shall exclusively refer to: New Year's Day, Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, the ninth of April, the first of May, the twelfth of June, the last Sunday of August, the thirtieth of November, the twenty-fifth and thirtieth of December. Nationwide special days shall include the first of November and the last day of December. As used in this Rule legal or regular holiday and special holiday shall now be referred to as 'regular holiday' and 'special day', respectively.

SECTION 4. Compensation for holiday work. — Any employee who is permitted or suffered to work on any regular holiday, not exceeding eight (8) hours, shall be paid at least two hundred percent (200%) of his regular daily wage. If the holiday work falls on the scheduled rest day of the employee, he shall be entitled to an additional premium pay of at least 30% of his regular holiday rate of 200% based on his regular wage rate.

SECTION 5. Overtime pay for holiday work. — For work performed in excess of eight hours on a regular holiday, an employee shall be paid an additional compensation for the overtime work equivalent to his rate for the first eight hours on such holiday work plus at least 30% thereof. Where the regular holiday work exceeding eight hours falls on the scheduled rest day of the employee, he shall be paid an additional compensation for the overtime work equivalent to his regular holiday-rest day for the first 8 hours plus 30% thereof. The regular holiday rest day rate of an employee shall consist of 200% of his regular daily wage rate plus 30% thereof.
explanation: The holiday-pay computation manual. Sec. 1 restates the Art. 82/94 exclusions — and David reads Sec. 1(e)'s task/commission phrase WITH 'field personnel' (ejusdem generis): task-basis workers get holiday pay unless they are field personnel. Sec. 2: monthly-paid employees (paid uniformly regardless of working days, at/above the 365/12 monthly minimum) are already paid for unworked holidays — no separate holiday pay accrues. Sec. 3: note its list is as stale as Art. 94(c) (last Sunday of August, no Eids) — use the EO 292-as-amended calendar. Secs. 4-5 build the rate ladder: worked regular holiday 200%; +rest day 260% (200% + 30% of 200%); OT on regular holiday = first-8-hours rate x 130%; OT on regular-holiday-rest-day = 260% x 130% = 338%. Remember: every holiday-work rate compounds on the rate beneath it.

citation: Omnibus Rules, Book III, Rule IV, Sec. 6
verbatim: SECTION 6. Absences. — (a) All covered employees shall be entitled to the benefit provided herein when they are on leave of absence with pay. Employees who are on leave of absence without pay on the day immediately preceding a regular holiday may not be paid the required holiday pay if he has not worked on such regular holiday. (b) Employees shall grant the same percentage of the holiday pay as the benefit granted by competent authority in the form of employee's compensation or social security payment, whichever is higher, if they are not reporting for work while on such benefits. (c) Where the day immediately preceding the holiday is a non-working day in the establishment or the scheduled rest day of the employee, he shall not be deemed to be on leave of absence on that day, in which case he shall be entitled to the holiday pay if he worked on the day immediately preceding the non-working day or rest day.
explanation: The syllabus 'Absences' item: holiday pay for an UNWORKED regular holiday depends on the day immediately preceding it. On leave WITH pay (or present) the day before = paid. Absent WITHOUT pay the day before = the employer MAY withhold holiday pay — UNLESS the employee actually works the holiday itself (working the holiday always earns the 200% rate). Paragraph (c) saves the worker when the preceding day is itself a non-working/rest day: entitlement then turns on the last actual workday before it. But paragraph (b) is an obvious textual corruption ('Employees shall grant...') — its sense (topping up EC/SSS benefits to the holiday-pay percentage) is noted but not examined. Practical application: HR systems must check the pre-holiday attendance code before releasing unworked-holiday pay. Remember: absence never forfeits pay for a holiday the employee WORKS.
