Thereafter, post-payment of the SSS grant or a reimbursement from SSS shall be made to the employer immediately upon receipt of satisfactory and legal proof of such payment for the maternity leave: Provided, That the SSS shall immediately reimburse the employer of one hundred percent (100%) of the amount of maternity benefits advanced to the female worker by the employer upon receipt of satisfactory and legal proof of such payment.

The maternity leave credits and benefits provided under this Act shall be granted to Kasambahays and female workers in the informal economy.

Women workers in the private sector covered by Republic Act No. 8282, otherwise known as the 'Social Security Act of 1997,' shall receive benefits equivalent to one hundred percent (100%) of their average daily salary credit for sixty (60) days in case of miscarriage or emergency termination of pregnancy, and one hundred (100) days in case of live childbirth, regardless of the mode of delivery, and an additional fifteen (15) days paid maternity leave shall also be granted to solo parents as defined under Republic Act No. 8972. An additional maternity leave of thirty (30) days, without pay, can be availed of, at the option of the female worker, without violating the security of tenure principle.

Maternity leave benefits granted under this Act shall be in lieu of any other similar maternity benefits that may be granted to pregnant female workers: Provided, That where other laws or collective bargaining agreements or employment contracts provide for maternity leave benefits more than those provided for under this Act, the female worker shall be entitled to such benefits.

Female workers availing of the maternity leave period and benefits must receive not less than two-thirds (2/3) of their regular monthly wages. For this purpose, employers from the private sector with female workers, who are voluntary SSS members while pregnant, shall remit all SSS contributions payments to the SSS in favor of the female workers and provide them their salary differentials.

The following are exempted from providing the salary differential requirements of this section: (1) Distressed establishments; (2) Retail/service establishments and other enterprises employing not more than ten (10) employees; (3) Microbusiness enterprises with total assets of not more than Three million pesos (P3,000,000.00); and (4) Enterprises already providing similar benefits, including benefits granted through collective bargaining agreements.

SEC. 6. Allocation of Maternity Leave Credits. - Any female worker entitled to maternity leave benefits as provided for herein may, at her option, allocate up to seven (7) days of said benefits to the child's father, whether or not the same is married to the female worker: Provided, That in the case of the death, absence, or incapacity of the father, the benefit may be allocated to an alternate caregiver who shall be either the current partner, whether or not the same is of the same sex as the female worker, or any of the grandparents, parents, siblings, and other relatives or qualified domestic caregivers: Provided, That written notice to the employers shall be given by the female worker and the alternate caregiver as well as the SSS: Provided, further, That this benefit shall be over and above that which is provided under Republic Act No. 8187, otherwise known as the 'Paternity Leave Act of 1996'. In the event the father or the alternate caregiver dies or becomes incapacitated, either before the 7-day leave or while on leave, said leave shall revert to the female worker.
explanation: The flagship leave law. Sec. 3: 105 DAYS with full pay per pregnancy (every pregnancy now — the old 4-pregnancy cap is gone), +30 optional unpaid, +15 for solo parents; miscarriage/emergency termination = 60 days. Secs. 4-5: public AND private (incl. kasambahays, informal economy) covered regardless of civil status/legitimacy/delivery mode. Private-sector mechanics: SSS member + 3 contributions in the 12 months before the semester of childbirth; employer ADVANCES full pay within 30 days of application, SSS reimburses 100%; employer pays the SALARY DIFFERENTIAL (full pay minus SSS grant) unless exempt (distressed, retail/service <=10, micro <=P3M assets, already-providing). Floor: at least 2/3 of regular monthly wages. Sec. 6: up to 7 days ALLOCABLE to the father (married or not) or, on his death/absence/incapacity, an alternate caregiver — OVER AND ABOVE RA 8187 paternity leave; reverts to the mother if the recipient dies/is incapacitated. Remember the 105/60/30/15/7 ladder and that benefits are 'in lieu of' lesser ones but yield to BETTER CBA/contract benefits.

citation: RA 8187, Secs. 2-3 (paternity leave grant and definition)
verbatim:
SECTION 2. Every married male employee in the private and public sectors shall be entitled to a paternity leave of seven (7) days with full pay for first four (4) deliveries of the legitimate spouse with whom he is cohabiting. The male employee shall apply for paternity leave by notifying his employer of his wife's pregnancy and his intention to avail of the benefits under this Act. Such application shall be supported by the physician's certification that the wife has indeed given birth or suffered a miscarriage; Provided, That delivery shall include childbirth, miscarriage, or abortion. Entitlement to paternity leave benefits under this Act for subsequent deliveries after the first four (4) shall be in accordance with the rules and regulations that the Secretary of Labor and Employment shall prescribe.

SECTION 3. For purposes of this Act, paternity leave shall mean the benefits granted to a married male employee allowing him to not report for work for seven (7) days but continues to earn the compensation therefor, on the condition that his spouse has delivered a child or suffered a miscarriage for purposes of enabling him to effectively lend support to his wife in her period of recovery and/or in the nursing of the newly-born child.
explanation: 7 days with full pay to MARRIED male employees (private + public) for the FIRST FOUR deliveries of the cohabiting legitimate spouse — delivery INCLUDES miscarriage/abortion, and entitlement needs notice + physician's certification. The syllabus cites Sec. 3 (the definition: paid non-reporting to support the wife's recovery and nurse the newborn); Sec. 2 supplies the grant and its limits. Two distinctions examiners test: (1) legitimacy/cohabitation conditions here vs. RA 11210 Sec. 6's allocation (no marriage requirement, over and above this Act); (2) the 4-delivery cap vs. maternity's every-pregnancy rule. Remember: paternity = married, 4 deliveries, 7 days; maternity allocation = any father/partner/relative, over and above.

citation: RA 9710, Sec. 18 (special leave benefits for women)
verbatim: SEC. 18. Special Leave Benefits for Women. - A woman employee having rendered continuous aggregate employment service of at least six (6) months for the last twelve (12) months shall be entitled to a special leave benefit of two (2) months with full pay based on her gross monthly compensation following surgery caused by gynecological disorders.
explanation: The 'gynecological leave': 2 MONTHS with full pay (based on GROSS monthly compensation) after surgery caused by gynecological disorders, requiring 6 months aggregate service in the last 12 months. Three limiters: (1) only female employees; (2) only SURGERY-caused (consultation/medication alone does not trigger it); (3) only gynecological disorders. Compare: maternity (RA 11210) pays via SSS + differential and needs no 6-month rule; this benefit is employer-paid at full gross pay. Remember: 2 months / surgery / gynecological / 6-in-12.

citation: RA 9262, Sec. 3(c) and Sec. 43 (battered woman syndrome; VAWC leave)
verbatim:
SECTION 3. Definition of Terms. — As used in this Act: [...] (c) 'Battered Woman Syndrome' refers to a scientifically defined pattern of psychological and behavioral symptoms found in women living in battering relationships as a result of cumulative abuse;

SECTION 43. Entitlement to Leave. — Victims under this Act shall be entitled to take a paid leave of absence up to ten (10) days in addition to other paid leaves under the Labor Code and Civil Service Rules and Regulations, extendible when the necessity arises as specified in the protection order. Any employer who shall prejudice the right of the person under this section shall be penalized in accordance with the provisions of the Labor Code and Civil Service Rules and Regulations. explanation: The VAWC leave: victims get up to 10 DAYS paid leave IN ADDITION to all other paid leaves (SIL, parental, etc. — it stacks, never substitutes), extendible per the protection order. BWS (Sec. 3(c)) is the defined psychological pattern of cumulative abuse — the provision's conceptual anchor and a justifying circumstance in the penal context (outside this module). Two employer duties: (1) grant the leave (prejudice is penalized under labor/CSC rules); (2) never prejudice co-employees who ASSIST a victim (liable for discrimination). Remember: 10 days / stacks on top / extendible via protection order / assistance-protection included.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 58 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 58. Definition of Terms. As used in this Title: (a) "Apprenticeship" means practical training on the job supplemented by related theoretical instruction. (b) An "apprentice" is a worker who is covered by a written apprenticeship agreement with an individual employer or any of the entities recognized under this Chapter. (c) An "apprenticeable occupation" means any trade, form of employment or occupation which requires more than three (3) months of practical training on the job supplemented by related theoretical instruction. (d) "Apprenticeship agreement" is an employment contract wherein the employer binds himself to train the apprentice and the apprentice in turn accepts the terms of training.
explanation: Four interlocking definitions. Apprenticeship = OJT PLUS related theoretical instruction (pure OJT without theory is not apprenticeship); an apprentice exists only under a WRITTEN apprenticeship agreement (no writing, no apprentice status — the worker defaults to regular employment analysis); an apprenticeable occupation needs MORE THAN 3 months of training (the 3-month line also separates apprentices from learners); and the agreement is itself an EMPLOYMENT contract (train-me / I-accept-training), so apprentices are employees with full labor-standards coverage except as the chapter provides. Practical application: TESDA/DOLE-approved programs and the written agreement are the employer's only proof of apprentice status in a regularization dispute. Remember: written + >3 months + theory = apprentice.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 59 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim:
ART. 59. Qualifications of Apprentice. To qualify as an apprentice, a person shall: (a) Be at least fourteen (14) years of age; (b) Possess vocational aptitude and capacity for appropriate tests; and (c) Possess the ability to comprehend and follow oral and written instructions.

Trade, industry and labor organizations may recommend to the Secretary of Labor and Employment appropriate educational requirements for different occupations.
explanation: Three qualifications: age 14+, vocational aptitude (testable), and ability to follow oral/written instructions. Currency note: the 14-year floor predates RA 9231 (2003), which now generally bars employment below 15 outside narrow family/non-hazardous exceptions — teach RA 9231 as the operative child-labor floor and Art. 59(a) as the chapter's internal rule (outside the syllabus citation, noted for accuracy). Industry/labor groups may recommend educational requirements through the Secretary. Remember: aptitude + comprehension are substantive — apprenticeship is training for the trainable, not cheap labor by another name.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 60 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 60. Employment of Apprentices. Only employers in the highly technical industries may employ apprentices and only in apprenticeable occupations approved by the Secretary of Labor and Employment.
explanation: The double gate on apprentice hiring: (1) the EMPLOYER must be in a highly technical industry, and (2) the OCCUPATION must be a Secretary-approved apprenticeable one. A retail shop or restaurant cannot 'hire apprentices' — the status is reserved for technical trades needing extended structured training. Enforcement consequence: workers hired as 'apprentices' outside these gates are analyzed as regular employees from day one. Remember: highly-technical-industry employer + approved occupation — fail either and the apprentice label collapses.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 61 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 61. Contents of Apprenticeship Agreements. Apprenticeship agreements, including the wage rates of apprentices, shall conform to the rules issued by the Secretary of Labor and Employment. The period of apprenticeship shall not exceed six (6) months. Apprenticeship agreements providing for wage rates below the legal minimum wage, which in no case shall start below 75 per cent of the applicable minimum wage, may be entered into only in accordance with apprenticeship programs duly approved by the Secretary of Labor and Employment. The Ministry shall develop standard model programs of apprenticeship.
explanation: Three controls: (1) the agreement must conform to Secretary rules (including wage rates); (2) the period CANNOT exceed 6 MONTHS — work beyond 6 months under the same arrangement converts toward regular employment; (3) sub-minimum apprentice wages are allowed ONLY within approved programs and NEVER below 75% of the applicable minimum wage — this is the syllabus's '61' under minimum wage. Compare: learners 75% (Art. 75(c)), PWDs 75% (Art. 80 par. 2), and Art. 124's auto-modification of training wage clauses on every wage increase. Practical application: calendar the 6-month expiry and re-verify the 75%-of-current-minimum floor after each wage order. Remember: 6 months max / 75% min / approved program only.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 72 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 72. Apprentices Without Compensation. The Secretary of Labor and Employment may authorize the hiring of apprentices without compensation whose training on the job is required by the school, training institution or curriculum, as approved by the appropriate government authority.
explanation: The ONLY unpaid apprenticeship: school/curriculum-required OJT, individually AUTHORIZED by the Secretary. Two cumulative conditions — (1) the training is required by the school/institution/curriculum as approved by government authority, AND (2) the Secretary authorizes the specific hiring. Without both, the 75% floor (Art. 61) applies. This is the practicum/OJT provision: it covers students earning academic credit, not 'trainees' doing productive work for free. Remember: unpaid requires school-requirement PLUS Secretary authorization — employer say-so alone never suffices.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 73 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 73. Definition of Learners. Learners are persons hired as trainees in semi-skilled and other industrial occupations which are non-apprenticeable and which may be learned through practical training on the job in a relatively short period of time which shall not exceed three (3) months.
explanation: The learner in one sentence: trainee + semi-skilled/non-apprenticeable occupation + OJT-learnable in <=3 MONTHS. The 3-month ceiling is the bright line against apprentices (>3 months + theory): learnership is for jobs learnable fast. 'Non-apprenticeable' means the occupation cannot qualify under Art. 58(c) — the two chapters are mutually exclusive by design. Remember: semi-skilled + non-apprenticeable + 3 months max = learner.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 74 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 74. When Learners May Be Hired. Learners may be employed when no experienced workers are available, the employment of learners is necessary to prevent curtailment of employment opportunities, and the employment does not create unfair competition in terms of labor costs or impair or lower working standards.
explanation: Three cumulative justifications for hiring learners: (1) no experienced workers AVAILABLE (a labor-market condition, not a preference); (2) NECESSARY to prevent curtailment of employment opportunities (training keeps jobs open); (3) no UNFAIR labor-cost competition and no impairment of working standards (learners cannot undercut regulars' wages/conditions). This is the anti-abuse gate: an employer fully staffed with experienced regulars cannot rotate 'learners' to save 25% on wages. Remember: unavailability + necessity + no-undercutting — all three, every time.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 75 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 75. Learnership Agreement. Any employer desiring to employ learners shall enter into a learnership agreement with them, which agreement shall include: (a) The names and addresses of the learners; (b) The duration of the learnership period, which shall not exceed three (3) months; (c) The wages or salary rates of the learners which shall begin at not less than seventy-five percent (75%) of the applicable minimum wages; and (d) A commitment to employ the learners if they so desire, as regular employees upon completion of the learnership. All learners who have been allowed or suffered to work during the first two (2) months shall be deemed regular employees if training is terminated by the employer before the end of the stipulated period through no fault of the learners.
explanation: The learnership agreement's four mandatory contents: names/addresses, duration (<=3 months), wage (>=75% of minimum — the syllabus's '75(c)' under minimum wage), and the COMMITMENT to hire as regulars on completion if they so desire. The sting is in the tail: learners allowed/suffered to work the first 2 months become REGULAR employees if the employer cuts training short through no fault of theirs — early termination converts status automatically. Compare apprentices: no parallel auto-regularization sentence exists in Arts. 58-61 (regularization follows general Art. 281/295 principles instead). Practical application: never terminate a learnership before month 3 without documented learner fault. Remember: 75% floor + hire-commitment + 2-month conversion tripwire.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 76 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 76. Learners in Piecework. Learners employed in piece or incremental work shall be paid in full for the work done.
explanation: One line with real bite: piece-rate learners get NO training discount — they are paid IN FULL for output. The 75% floor of Art. 75(c) governs time-rated learnership; once pay is per piece, the learner earns the full piece rate from day one. Rationale: piece rates already self-adjust for inexperience (slower hands earn less). Remember: time-learners 75%, piece-learners 100%.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 78 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 78. Definition. Handicapped workers are those whose earning capacity is impaired by age or physical or mental deficiency or injury.
explanation: The chapter's gateway definition: earning capacity IMPAIRED by age, physical/mental deficiency, or injury. Terminology note: the Code says 'handicapped workers'; current usage (RA 7277 onward) is persons with disabilities (PWDs) — the syllabus itself uses 'PWDs (78-81)'. The definition's pivot is IMPAIRED EARNING CAPACITY, not the disability label alone — which is why Art. 79 tests employability against the specific work. Remember: impairment + earning-capacity effect = chapter coverage.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 79 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 79. When Employable. Handicapped workers may be employed when their employment is necessary to prevent curtailment of employment opportunities and when it does not create unfair competition in labor costs or impair or lower working standards.
explanation: The PWD twin of Art. 74's learner gate: employment must be NECESSARY to prevent curtailment of opportunities AND must not undercut labor costs or working standards. Same anti-abuse logic — the sub-minimum wage permission (Art. 80 par. 2) exists to OPEN jobs, never to cheapen them. Note the deliberate omission versus Art. 74: no 'no experienced workers available' condition — PWD hiring is encouraged even where experienced workers exist. Remember: necessity + no-undercutting (no unavailability requirement).

citation: Labor Code, Art. 80 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim:
ART. 80. Employment Agreement. Any employer who employs handicapped workers shall enter into an employment agreement with them, which agreement shall include: (a) The names and addresses of the handicapped workers to be employed; (b) The rate to be paid the handicapped workers which shall not be less than seventy five (75%) percent of the applicable legal minimum wage; (c) The duration of employment period; and (d) The work to be performed by handicapped workers.

The employment agreement shall be subject to inspection by the Secretary of Labor and Employment or his duly authorized representatives.
explanation: Four mandatory contents mirroring learnership: names, rate (>=75% of legal minimum — the syllabus's '80 par. 2' under minimum wage), duration, and the work to be performed. The inspection sentence makes the agreement a DOLE-auditable document (cf. Art. 128(a)). Pair with Art. 81: PWDs meeting apprentice/learner qualifications train under THOSE chapters' rules — Art. 80 governs PWDs hired as workers, not trainees. Practical application: keep the written agreement on file at the workplace (Rule X Sec. 11 logic) with the 75% floor recomputed per current wage order. Remember: same four corners as learnership, but for employment rather than training.

citation: Labor Code, Art. 81 (renumbered; same number as original)
verbatim: ART. 81. Eligibility for Apprenticeship. Subject to the appropriate provisions of this Code, handicapped workers may be hired as apprentices or learners if their handicap is not such as to effectively impede the performance of job operations in the particular occupations for which they are hired.
explanation: The bridge article: PWDs may train as APPRENTICES or LEARNERS whenever the handicap does not effectively impede the particular job's operations — channeling them into Arts. 58-72 (with theory, >3 months, 6-month cap) or Arts. 73-76 (semi-skilled, <=3 months, hire-commitment) as the occupation fits. The test is job-specific ('in the particular occupations'), not categorical: a mobility impairment barring warehouse apprenticeship is irrelevant to a desk-based learnership. RA 7277 Sec. 7 restates the same eligibility for the modern regime. Remember: Art. 81 routes PWD TRAINEES to the apprentice/learner chapters; Arts. 78-80 govern PWD WORKERS.

verbatim: SECTION 5. Equal Opportunity for Employment. — No disabled persons shall be denied access to opportunities for suitable employment. A qualified disabled employee shall be subject to the same terms and conditions of employment and the same compensation, privileges, benefits, fringe benefits, incentives or allowances as a qualified able-bodied person.
explanation: The modern PWD employment rule sitting alongside Arts. 78-81: no denial of SUITABLE employment, and — once qualified — IDENTICAL terms, compensation, and benefits as able-bodied counterparts. The apparent tension with Art. 80's 75% floor resolves by scope: Art. 80's training-period rate applies during the covered employment-agreement period; Sec. 5 governs qualified PWD employees generally (equal pay for equal work — cf. Art. 133(a)'s 'work of equal value' logic). RA 7277 Sec. 6 reserves 5% of casual/emergency/contractual posts in listed social-development agencies for PWDs; Sec. 7 confirms apprenticeship eligibility. Later amendments (RA 9442, RA 10754) touched only privileges/discounts — this section stands as enacted. Remember: suitable-employment access + qualified-employee equality.

verbatim:
Section 1. There is hereby created a Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation hereinafter referred to as the 'Corporation' which shall insure as herein provided, the deposits of all banks which are entitled to the benefits of insurance under this Act, and which shall have the powers hereinafter granted.

The Corporation shall, as a basic policy, promote and safeguard the interests of the depositing public by providing insurance coverage on all insured deposits and helping maintain a sound and stable banking system.

The Corporation shall be attached to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas for policy and program coordination.
explanation: PDIC is a government instrumentality created by statute (RA 3591, approved 22 June 1963) to insure bank deposits. Its basic policy is twin: protect depositors and help keep the banking system sound and stable. Since RA 11840 it is attached to the BSP for policy and program coordination, but it remains a separate corporate body that can sue and be sued. Practical point: deposit insurance is automatic and mandatory — the depositor neither applies for it nor pays a premium; the bank pays assessments to PDIC.

verbatim:
SEC. 2. It is hereby declared to be the policy of the State to strengthen the mandatory deposit insurance coverage system to generate, preserve, maintain faith and confidence in the country's banking system, and protect it from illegal schemes and machinations.

Towards this end, the government must extend all means and mechanisms necessary for the Corporation to effectively fulfill its vital task of promoting and safeguarding the interests of the depositing public by way of providing insurance coverage on bank deposits and in helping develop a sound and stable banking system.

In view of the crucial role and the nature of its functions and responsibilities, the Corporation, while being a government instrumentality with corporate powers, shall enjoy fiscal and administrative autonomy.
explanation: Three ideas to memorize: (1) deposit insurance is MANDATORY, not optional; (2) its purpose is faith and confidence in banks plus protection against illegal schemes; (3) PDIC enjoys fiscal and administrative autonomy because its role is crucial. Exam point: when asked why PDIC can act quickly (take over banks, pay claims), anchor on this State policy plus the autonomy clause.

citation: RA 3591, Sec. 3(a) (as amended by RA 11840; quorum retained from RA 10846)
explanation: The PDIC Board has SEVEN members: the BSP Governor as Chair, the Finance Secretary as Vice-Chair, the PDIC President, and four private-sector appointive directors (6-year terms, one reappointment only). The middle of paragraph (4) on staggered first appointments and performance scores is omitted above. Remember: quorum and decision rule is FOUR. The Board holds the charter's key levers — it sets the assessment rate, raises the MDIC, and directs receivership and liquidation. Practical point: major PDIC actions (e.g., the 2025 MDIC increase) are Board actions, which is why they cite Board authority.

verbatim:
Section 6. The deposit liabilities of any bank which is engaged in the business of receiving deposits as herein defined on the effective date of this Act, or which thereafter may engage in the business of receiving deposits, shall be insured with the Corporation. The Corporation may establish separate insurance funds and insurance arrangements or structures or takaful that take into consideration the peculiar characteristics of Islamic banking.

Whenever a bank is determined by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas to be capital deficient, the Corporation may conduct an insurance risk evaluation on the bank to enable it to assess the risks to the DIF. Such evaluation may include the determination of: (i) the fair market value of the assets and liabilities of a bank; or (ii) the risk classification of a bank.
explanation: This is the DUTY TO INSURE: every bank that takes deposits MUST be insured with PDIC — no bank may opt out, and coverage attaches by operation of law. The 2022 amendment adds Islamic-banking windows (separate funds or takaful) and lets PDIC run an insurance-risk evaluation (fair value of assets and liabilities, risk classification) once BSP finds a bank capital deficient — an early-warning tool that protects the Deposit Insurance Fund before closure. Remember: the duty runs between the BANK and PDIC; the depositor is the beneficiary and pays nothing.

verbatim:
The assessment rate shall be determined by the Board of Directors: Provided, That the assessment rate shall not exceed one-fifth (1/5) of one per centum (1%) per annum. The semi-annual assessment for each insured bank shall be in the amount of the product of one-half (1/2) the assessment rate multiplied by the assessment base but in no case shall it be less than Five thousand pesos (P5,000.00). The assessment base shall be the amount of the liability of the bank for deposits as defined under subsection (g) of Section 5 without any deduction for indebtedness of depositors.

[...]

In case there will be an increase in the maximum deposit insurance coverage, the PDIC Board shall have the authority to adjust the assessment rate for banks taking into consideration the current economic conditions, and the adequacy and sustainability of the DIF.
explanation: Banks fund deposit insurance through assessments: the Board sets the rate (ceiling 1/5 of 1% per year), each bank pays semi-annually on its total deposit liabilities with NO deduction for what depositors owe the bank, and no bank pays less than P5,000 per half-year. The omitted middle paragraph requires a Board study on a risk-based assessment system. The last paragraph links funding to coverage: if the MDIC rises (as it did in 2025), the Board may adjust the rate to keep the DIF adequate and sustainable. Exam point: assessment base is GROSS deposit liabilities — a bank cannot net out borrowers' loans.

citation: RA 3591, Sec. 9, Eighth, Ninth, and Fourteenth powers (as amended by RA 11840)
verbatim:
Eighth - To examine the records and books of accounts and require information and reports from depository institutions in case there is a finding of fraud or unsafe or unsound banking related to deposit-taking: Provided, That, notwithstanding the provisions of Republic Act No. 1405, as amended, Republic Act No. 6426, as amended, Republic Act No. 8791, and other laws, the Corporation and/or the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, may inquire into or examine deposit accounts and all information related thereto in case there is a finding of unsafe or unsound banking practice: Provided, further, That to avoid overlapping of efforts, the examination shall maximize the efficient use of the relevant reports, information, and findings of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, which it shall make available to the Corporation.

[...]

Ninth - To act as receiver.

[...]

Fourteenth - To determine the appropriate mode of liquidation of a closed bank and to implement the same.
explanation: Three charter powers to memorize. (1) Examination: on a finding of fraud or deposit-related unsafe/unsound banking, PDIC may examine books and even deposit accounts despite the secrecy laws (RA 1405, RA 6426, RA 8791) — a narrow statutory exception, coordinated with BSP to avoid duplication. (2) Receiver: the two-word grant behind PDIC's takeover of every closed bank (detailed in Secs. 12-14). (3) Liquidation mode: PDIC alone chooses conventional liquidation or purchase-and-assumption and implements it. The omitted powers (seal, succession, contracts, suit, personnel, by-laws, compromise of claims, provident fund) are standard corporate-housekeeping grants.

citation: RA 3591, Sec. 5(g) (as amended by RA 10846 and RA 11840)
verbatim:
(g) The term deposit means the unpaid balance of money or its equivalent received by a bank in the usual course of business and for which it has given or is obliged to give credit to a commercial, checking, savings, time or thrift account, evidenced by a passbook, certificate of deposit, or other evidence of deposit issued in accordance with Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas rules and regulations and other applicable laws, together with such other obligations of a bank, which, consistent with banking usage and practices, the Board of Directors shall determine and prescribe by regulations to be deposit liabilities of the bank: Provided, That any obligation of a bank which is payable at the office of the bank located outside of the Philippines shall not be a deposit for any of the purposes of this Act or included as part of the total deposits or of insured deposit: Provided, further, That subject to the approval of the Board of Directors, any insured bank which is incorporated under the laws of the Philippines which maintains a branch outside the Philippines may elect to include for insurance its deposit obligations payable only at such branch.

Certain products or arrangements of Islamic banks shall be deemed as deposit by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas for purposes of this Act.

The Corporation shall not pay deposit insurance for the following accounts or transactions:

(1) Investment products such as bonds and securities, trust accounts, and other similar instruments;

(2) Deposit accounts or transactions which are fictitious or fraudulent as determined by the Corporation;

(3) Deposit accounts or transactions constituting unsafe and unsound banking, as determined by the Corporation, in consultation with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, after due notice and hearing, and publication of a directive to cease and desist issued by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas against such deposit accounts, transactions or unsafe and unsound banking; and

(4) Deposits that are determined to be the proceeds of an unlawful activity as defined under Republic Act No. 9160, as amended.

The actions of the Corporation taken under Section 5(g) shall be final and executory, and may only be restrained or set aside by the Court of Appeals, upon appropriate petition for certiorari on the ground that the action was taken in excess of jurisdiction or with such grave abuse of discretion as to amount to a lack or excess of jurisdiction. The petition for certiorari may only be filed within thirty (30) days from notice of denial of claim for deposit insurance.
explanation: The heart of deposit insurance. A deposit exists only if the BANK RECEIVED money or its equivalent in the usual course of business — no receipt, no deposit, no insurance (this is why the Supreme Court absolved PDIC in PDIC v. CA and Chugani). Offshore-payable obligations are excluded, but a Philippine bank's foreign branch may opt its branch deposits in with Board approval. Four accounts are NEVER paid: (1) investments, trust accounts and the like; (2) fictitious or fraudulent accounts as PDIC determines; (3) unsafe/unsound-banking accounts after due process and a published BSP cease-and-desist directive; (4) money-laundering proceeds under RA 9160. PDIC's rulings here are final and executory — challengeable only by certiorari to the COURT OF APPEALS within 30 days from denial notice, and only for grave abuse of discretion.

verbatim:
(k) The term insured deposit means the amount due to any bonafide depositor for legitimate deposits in an insured bank as of the date of closure but not to exceed Five hundred thousand pesos (P500,000.00). Such amount shall be determined according to such regulations as the Board of Directors may prescribe. In determining such amount due to any depositor, there shall be added together all deposits in the bank maintained in the same right and capacity for his or her benefit either in his or her own name or in the name of others. A joint account regardless of whether the conjunction 'and', 'or', 'and/or' is used, shall be insured separately from any individually-owned deposit account: Provided, That (1) if the account is held jointly by two or more natural persons, or by two or more juridical persons or entities, the maximum insured deposit shall be divided into as many equal shares as there are individuals, juridical persons or entities, unless a different sharing is stipulated in the document of deposit, and (2) if the account is held by a juridical person or entity jointly with one or more natural persons, the maximum insured deposit shall be presumed to belong entirely to such juridical person or entity: Provided, further, That the aggregate of the interest of each co-owner over several joint accounts, whether owned by the same or different combinations of individuals, juridical persons or entities, shall likewise be subject to the maximum insured deposit: Provided, furthermore, That the provisions of any law to the contrary notwithstanding, no owner/holder of any passbook, certificate of deposit or other evidence of deposit shall be recognized as a depositor entitled to the rights provided in this Act unless the passbook, certificate of deposit or other evidence of deposit is determined by the Corporation to be an authentic document or record of the issuing bank.

In case a condition occurs that threatens the monetary and financial stability of the banking system that may have systemic consequences, as defined in Section 22 hereof, and as determined by the Monetary Board, the maximum deposit insurance cover may be adjusted in such amount, for such a period, and/or for such deposit products, as may be determined by a unanimous vote of the Board of Directors in a meeting called for the purpose and chaired by the Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas or the designated alternate, subject to the approval of the President of the Philippines.

The Board of Directors may increase the amount of the maximum deposit insurance coverage to an amount indexed to inflation or in consideration of other economic indicators as may be deemed appropriate by the Board. The Board of Directors shall review the amount of the maximum deposit insurance coverage every three (3) years and increase the maximum deposit insurance coverage as may be warranted. In the exercise of this authority, the Board may consider economic indicators other than inflation. For this purpose, the Board may hire the services of independent actuarial consultants and other experts to determine the feasibility and advisability of increasing the maximum deposit insurance coverage.
explanation: Read this together with the 2025 MDIC increase. The statute still prints P500,000, but the third paragraph lets the BOARD raise the MDIC (indexed to inflation or other indicators, reviewed every 3 years) — and the Board did: P1,000,000 per depositor per bank effective 15 March 2025 (Memo No. 2025-01). So P500,000 is the statutory floor text; P1M is the CURRENT payable maximum. Aggregation rules: add all deposits held in the SAME right and capacity; joint accounts are insured SEPARATELY from individual accounts; co-owners split the maximum equally unless the deposit document says otherwise; a juridical-plus-natural joint account is presumed to belong entirely to the juridical person; and only AUTHENTIC bank records count (fake or replica documents are not deposits). The second paragraph is the emergency lever: on systemic threat as determined by the Monetary Board, the Board by UNANIMOUS vote (chaired by the BSP Governor) may adjust cover temporarily, subject to Presidential approval.

verbatim:
Effective 15 March 2025, the Maximum Deposit Insurance Coverage provided by the Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation (PDIC) is increased to One Million Pesos (P1,000,000.00) per depositor, per bank.

[...]

Upon effectivity of the new MDIC, banks shall prominently display the new Official PDIC Digital Decal in its official website, official social media pages, digital channels, mobile applications, ATMs and other similar machines, and include in its general advertisements and advertisement of deposit products the new Insurance Statement: "Deposits are insured by PDIC up to P1 Million per depositor."
explanation: The CURRENT rule on coverage. Since 15 March 2025, every bona fide depositor in every insured bank is covered up to P1,000,000 — the first increase since 2009 (P500,000 under RA 9576), and the first ever done by Board action under the Sec. 5(k) authority rather than by a new statute. History ladder for context: P10,000 (1963) → P15,000 (1978) → P40,000 (1984) → P100,000 (1992) → P250,000 (2004) → P500,000 (2009) → P1,000,000 (2025). Trap: any problem citing P500,000 as the current maximum is OUTDATED — use P1M for closures on or after 15 March 2025. Banks must now display the digital decal and the exact insurance statement quoted above.

citation: IRR of RA 11840, Rule III, Sec. 3(b)
verbatim:
Deposit accounts or transactions which are fictitious or fraudulent, as determined by the Corporation.

1. A deposit account or transaction shall be deemed fictitious when it is simulated, feigned, or not a genuine deposit account or transaction [e.g., Money or Equivalent (of money) was made to appear to have been received by a bank, or deposit account or the name of the depositor does not appear in the records of the bank], or unfunded, [i.e., no money or equivalent (of money) is received by a bank for such account or transaction], or deposit account or the name of the depositor does not appear in the records of the bank.

2. A deposit account or transaction shall be deemed fraudulent whenever the bank and/or depositor knowingly employ means calculated to deceive, including acts, omissions and concealment involving a breach of legal or equitable duty, trust, or confidence justly reposed, resulting in damage to another, or by which an undue and unconscientious advantage is taken of another, e.g., the named depositor denies ownership of the deposit.
explanation: How to tell the two apart. FICTITIOUS = the deposit is not real: simulated, unfunded (nothing actually reached the bank), or absent from bank records. FRAUDULENT = someone knowingly schemed to deceive (e.g., a depositor who denies owning the account booked in her name, or replica certificates like in Chugani). Transcribed from the PDIC-published signed PDF with only line-break spacing normalized; the repeated records clause in item 1 appears in the published text. Practical point: PDIC decides this itself in the first instance, and its denial is final and executory subject only to CA certiorari within 30 days.

citation: IRR of RA 11840, Rule III, Sec. 3(a) and (d)
verbatim:
The following features may be considered as grounds for determining that a product is an investment:

1. No debtor-creditor relationship exists between the bank and the client;

2. Relationship between the bank and the client is either that of a trustee-trustor or agent-principal;

3. Principal amount is not protected;

4. Amount deposited is not withdrawable on demand; and/or

5. Other analogous features.

[...]

Payment of deposit insurance shall be deferred on any deposit which is the subject matter of any freeze order, civil forfeiture proceeding, money laundering case, or any other case, or any other case involving an Unlawful Activity, pending before the Department of Justice, Office of the Ombudsman, or the regular courts.

Deposit insurance payments shall only be made upon a final judgment effectively holding that the deposits do not constitute proceeds of an Unlawful Activity.

Deposits determined with finality by the courts to be proceeds of an Unlawful Activity shall not be paid deposit insurance.

If a deposit insurance claim is denied, the concerned depositor may file within sixty (60) days from receipt of the denial, a verified request for reconsideration based on new evidence, together with affidavit/s and other document/s in support of the claim.
explanation: Two exclusion mechanics. INVESTMENTS: the test is substance over label — if there is no debtor-creditor relationship (trustee, agent, at-risk principal, lock-up), the product is an investment even if the bank called it a deposit. MONEY-LAUNDERING PROCEEDS: PDIC DEFERS payment while a freeze/forfeiture/MLA case is pending, pays only on a final judgment clearing the deposit, and never pays what courts finally adjudge as unlawful-activity proceeds. Lifeline for denied claimants: a verified request for reconsideration on NEW evidence within 60 days from denial — distinct from the 30-day CA certiorari remedy. Transcribed from the signed PDF with only line-break spacing normalized; the doubled phrase in the deferral sentence appears in the published text.

verbatim:
The penalty of imprisonment of not less than six (6) years but not more than twelve (12) years or a fine of not less than Fifty thousand pesos (P50,000.00) but not more than Ten million pesos (P10,000,000.00), or both, at the discretion of the court, shall be imposed upon:

(1) Any director, officer, employee or agent of a bank for:

[...]

(e) Splitting of deposits or creation of fictitious or fraudulent loans or deposit accounts.

Splitting of deposits occurs whenever a deposit account with an outstanding balance of more than the statutory maximum amount of insured deposit maintained under the name of natural or juridical persons is broken down and transferred into two (2) or more accounts in the name/s of natural or juridical persons or entities who have no beneficial ownership on transferred deposits in their names within one hundred twenty (120) days immediately preceding or during a bank-declared bank holiday, or immediately preceding a closure order issued by the Monetary Board of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas for the purpose of availing of the maximum deposit insurance coverage;
explanation: Splitting = breaking one big account into several small ones in the names of NON-OWNERS (no beneficial ownership) within 120 days before a bank holiday or MB closure order, to multiply insurance coverage. Elements to check: (1) source balance above the maximum; (2) break-up into 2+ accounts; (3) transferees who are not real owners; (4) inside the 120-day window; (5) purpose of maxing out coverage. Consequence is double: the split claims are DENIED (see So v. PDIC, where a son's account traced to the Reyes family mother account), and the bank insiders face 6-12 years imprisonment and/or P50,000-P10,000,000 fine. Trap: the window is 120 days (RA 9576), not 30 — the 30-day figure in old materials is obsolete.

verbatim: SEC. 12. (a) Whenever a bank is ordered closed by the Monetary Board, the Corporation shall be designated as receiver and it shall proceed with the takeover and liquidation of the closed bank in accordance with this Act. For this purpose, banks closed by the Monetary Board shall no longer be rehabilitated.
explanation: Closure triggers a fixed chain: Monetary Board closure order → PDIC automatically becomes RECEIVER → takeover → liquidation. Two absolutes: PDIC is ALWAYS the receiver (no other receiver may be appointed), and a closed bank can NEVER be rehabilitated or reopened — liquidation is the only destination. Exam point: distinguish closure (MB's BSP-law act, reviewable only for arbitrariness/bad faith per Central Bank v. CA) from receivership/liquidation (PDIC's charter domain).

citation: RA 3591, Sec. 13(a)-(c) (as inserted by RA 10846; Sec. 13(b)(3) as amended by RA 11840)
explanation: PDIC as receiver needs NOBODY's consent — not stockholders, directors, creditors, or depositors — to pick conventional liquidation, purchase-and-assumption, or a mix. Core powers quoted above: step into the bank's shoes, gather everything, convert assets to cash (including FISTC bulk sales of bad assets under RA 11523, added 2022), sue insiders and collect loans (with power to modify or compromise terms), cut unreasonably high deposit-interest rates (earned-but-unpaid interest only), and distribute under the Civil Code concurrence-and-preference ladder. Omitted items (5)-(7), (9)-(10), (12)-(13), (15)-(16) cover deputies and forensic investigators, 3-month utilities/salaries, private counsel, borrowing against bank assets, court-approved liquidation fees, records disposal, and residual powers. After all claims are paid, SURPLUS dividends at the legal rate run from takeover to distribution — only then do stockholders get anything.

verbatim:
(e) The placement of a bank under liquidation shall have the following effects:

(1) On the corporate franchise or existence. Upon placement by the Monetary Board of a bank under liquidation, it shall continue as a body corporate until the termination of the winding-up period under Section 16 of this Act. Such continuation as a body corporate shall only be for the purpose of liquidating, settling and closing its affairs and for the disposal, conveyance or distribution of its assets pursuant to this Act. The receiver shall represent the closed bank in all cases by or against the closed bank and prosecute and defend suits by or against it. In no case shall the bank be reopened and permitted to resume banking business after being placed under liquidation.

(2) On the powers and functions of its directors, officers and stockholders. The powers, voting rights, functions and duties, as well as the allowances, remuneration and perquisites of the directors, officers, and stockholders of such bank are terminated upon its closure. Accordingly, the directors, officers, and stockholders shall be barred from interfering in any way with the assets, records, and affairs of the bank.

(3) On the assets. Upon service of notice of closure as provided in Section 14 of this Act, all the assets of the closed bank shall be deemed in custodia legis in the hands of the receiver, and as such, these assets may not be subject to attachment, garnishment, execution, levy or any other court processes.

[...]

(4) On labor relations. Notwithstanding the provisions of the Labor Code, the employer-employee relationship between the closed bank and its employees shall be deemed terminated upon service of the notice of closure of the bank in accordance with this Act. Payment of separation pay or benefits provided for by law shall be made from available assets of the bank in accordance with the Rules on Concurrence and Preference of Credits under the Civil Code or other laws.

[...]

(6) On interest payments. The liability of a bank to pay interest on deposits and all other obligations as of closure shall cease upon its closure by the Monetary Board without prejudice to the first paragraph of Section 85 of Republic Act No. 7653 (the New Central Bank Act).
explanation: Liquidation freezes the bank in five quoted dimensions: (1) the bank survives as a corporation ONLY to wind up — never to reopen; (2) directors, officers, and stockholders lose all powers and pay and must not interfere; (3) assets enter custodia legis — no attachment, garnishment, execution, or levy (a judge who issues one anyway is liable); (4) all employer-employee relations end by operation of law, with separation pay ranked under concurrence-and-preference; (6) interest STOPS running at closure. Omitted effects (5), (7)-(14) cover contract repudiation, tax-penalty relief, post-closure service fees, 180-day suspension of pending actions for mediation, stay of execution of final judgments, deferred docket fees, presumptions of ownership and regularity, and COA visitorial audit. Remember: closure-date interest cut-off is why insured deposits are computed AS OF closure.

verbatim:
SEC. 14. (a) Upon the designation of the Corporation as receiver of a closed bank, it shall serve a notice of closure to the highest-ranking officer of the bank present in the bank premises, or in the absence of such officer, post the notice of closure in the bank premises or on its main entrance. The closure of the bank shall be deemed effective upon the service of the notice of closure. Thereafter, the receiver shall takeover the bank and exercise the powers of the receiver as provided in this Act.

[...]

(c) Directors, officers, employees or agents of a bank hold money and other assets of the bank in trust or under administration or management by them for the bank in their fiduciary capacity.

Upon service of the notice of closure to the bank, all directors, officers, employees or agents of the closed bank shall have the duty to immediately account for, surrender and turn over to the receiver, and provide information relative to, the assets, records, and affairs of the closed bank in their possession, custody, administration or management.
explanation: Takeover mechanics in two steps: SERVE the notice of closure on the highest-ranking officer present (or post it if none is around) — closure takes effect at that moment — then TAKE OVER. Bank insiders hold everything in TRUST and must immediately account for and surrender all assets, records, and affairs plus information. The omitted paragraphs let the receiver use reasonable force (including forcing premises open) and call on LGUs and law enforcement for assistance. Exam point: closure is effective upon SERVICE of notice, not upon the MB resolution date or publication.

verbatim:
(g) A petition for assistance in the liquidation is a special proceeding for the liquidation of a closed bank, and includes the declaration of the concomitant right of its creditors and the order of payment of their valid claims in the disposition of its assets.

Any proceeding initiated under this section shall be considered in rem. Jurisdiction over all persons affected by the proceeding shall be considered as acquired upon publication of the order setting the case for initial hearing in any newspaper of general circulation in the Philippines.

[...]

(l) All persons or entities with claims against the assets of the closed bank shall file their claims with the receiver within sixty (60) days from the date of publication of the notice of closure. Claims filed outside the foregoing prescribed period shall be disallowed.

Claims denied by the receiver shall be filed with the liquidation court within sixty (60) days from receipt of the final notice of denial of claim.
explanation: The liquidation court track. PDIC files an ex parte PETITION FOR ASSISTANCE in the RTC (of the bank's or receiver's principal office, at PDIC's option) — an IN REM special proceeding, so publication of the initial-hearing order binds everyone. The liquidation court has EXCLUSIVE jurisdiction over disputed claims. Two 60-day clocks: (1) ALL claims against bank assets go to the RECEIVER within 60 days from publication of the closure notice (late = disallowed); (2) receiver-denied claims go to the LIQUIDATION COURT within 60 days from final denial notice. Do not confuse with the insurance track: insured-deposit claims follow Sec. 21 (2-year bar), and Sec. 5(g) denials go to the CA by certiorari within 30 days. Winding up: creditors and stockholders get 6 months from publication of the approved final distribution plan to claim; unclaimed assets go to the Bureau of Treasury.

verbatim: SEC. 19. Whenever an insured bank shall have been closed by the Monetary Board pursuant to Section 30 of Republic Act No. 7653, or upon expiration or revocation of a bank's corporate term, payment of the insured deposits on such closed bank shall be made by the Corporation as soon as possible either (1) by cash or (2) by making available to each depositor a transferred deposit in another insured bank in an amount equal to insured deposit of such depositor: Provided, however, That the Corporation, in its discretion, may require proof of claims to be filed before paying the insured deposits, and that in any case where the Corporation is not satisfied as to the validity of a claim for an insured deposit, it may require final determination of a court of competent jurisdiction before paying such claim: Provided, further, That failure to settle the claim, within six (6) months from the date of filing of claim for insured deposit, where such failure was due to grave abuse of discretion, gross negligence, bad faith, or malice, shall, upon conviction, subject the directors, officers or employees of the Corporation responsible for the delay, to imprisonment from six (6) months to one (1) year: Provided, furthermore, That the period shall not apply if the validity of the claim requires the resolution of issues of facts and or law by another office, body or agency including the case mentioned in the first proviso or by the Corporation together with such other office, body or agency.
explanation: Payment duty and modes. PDIC pays insured deposits AS SOON AS POSSIBLE after MB closure (or corporate-term expiry/revocation) either in CASH or as a TRANSFERRED DEPOSIT in another insured bank. PDIC may require proof of claim first, and may hold out for a court's final determination when validity is doubtful. The 6-month settlement clock has teeth: delay caused by grave abuse, gross negligence, bad faith, or malice jails the responsible PDIC personnel (6 months to 1 year) — unless the claim genuinely needs another office or agency to resolve factual or legal issues. Practical point: 'as soon as possible' plus the 6-month rule is why PDIC runs payout operations immediately after takeover.

verbatim: SEC. 20. The Corporation, upon payment of any depositor as provided for in Section 19 of this Act, shall be subrogated to all rights of the depositor against the closed bank to the extent of such payment. Such subrogation shall include the right on the part of the Corporation to receive the same dividends and payments from the proceeds of the assets of such closed bank and recoveries on account of stockholders' liability as would have been payable to the depositor on a claim for the insured deposits: Provided, That such depositor shall retain his or her claim for any uninsured portion of his or her deposit, which legal preference shall be the same as that of the subrogated claim of the Corporation for its payment of insured deposits. All payments by the Corporation of insured deposits in closed banks partake of the nature of public funds, and as such, must be considered a preferred credit in the order of preference under Article 2244 (9) of the New Civil Code.
explanation: Pay and step in. The moment PDIC pays a depositor, it is SUBROGATED — it takes over that depositor's rights against the bank up to the amount paid, including dividends from asset proceeds and stockholder-liability recoveries. The depositor keeps the UNINSURED excess, and — key 2016 improvement — that excess enjoys the SAME legal preference as PDIC's subrogated claim. Because payouts are PUBLIC FUNDS, PDIC's claim is a PREFERRED CREDIT under Civil Code Article 2244(9). Worked example: Ana has P1.5M in a bank closed in 2025. PDIC pays P1M (current MDIC) and is subrogated for P1M; Ana keeps a P500,000 uninsured claim with equal preference — both share in liquidation dividends ahead of ordinary unsecured creditors.

citation: RA 3591, Sec. 21(a), (b), (d), (e) (as renumbered by RA 10846; text from RA 9302)
verbatim:
(a) The Corporation shall commence the determination of insured deposits due the depositors of a closed bank upon its actual takeover of the closed bank. The Corporation shall give notice to the depositors of the closed bank of the insured deposits due them by whatever means deemed appropriate by the Board of Directors: Provided, That the Corporation shall publish the notice once a week for at least three (3) consecutive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation or, when appropriate, in a newspaper circulated in the community or communities where the closed bank or its branches are located.

(b) Payment of an insured deposit to any person by the Corporation shall discharge the Corporation, and payment of a transferred deposit to any person by the new bank or by an insured bank in which a transferred deposit has been made available shall discharge the Corporation and such new bank or other insured bank, to the same extent that payment to such person by the closed bank would have discharged it from liability for the insured deposit.

[... (c) omitted: unrecorded part-owners need not be recognized if recognition would inflate aggregate insured deposits ...]

(d) The Corporation may withhold payment of such portion of the insured deposit of any depositor in a closed bank as may be required to provide for the payment of any liability of such depositor as a stockholder of the closed bank, or of any liability of such depositor to the closed bank or its receiver, which is not offset against a claim due from such bank, pending the determination and payment of such liability by such depositor or any other liable therefor.

(e) Unless otherwise waived by the Corporation, if the depositor in the closed bank shall fail to claim his insured deposits with the Corporation within two (2) years from actual takeover of the closed bank by the receiver, or does not enforce his claim filed with the corporation within two (2) years after the two-year period to file a claim as mentioned hereinabove, all rights of the depositor against the Corporation with respect to the insured deposit shall be barred; however, all rights of the depositor against the closed bank and its shareholders or the receivership estate to which the Corporation may have become subrogated, shall thereupon revert to the depositor. Thereafter, the Corporation shall be discharged from any liability on the insured deposit.
explanation: The insurance-claims track, step by step. (a) Determination starts at ACTUAL TAKEOVER, and PDIC must publish notice to depositors once a week for 3 straight weeks. (b) Proper payment DISCHARGES PDIC (and the transferee bank) exactly as if the closed bank itself had paid. (d) PDIC may WITHHOLD what a depositor owes as stockholder or borrower pending determination — setoff protection for the estate. (e) The double 2-year bar: claim within 2 years from takeover, then enforce a filed claim within the next 2 years, or lose the PDIC remedy (the claim against the bank/estate itself reverts to the depositor). Trap: this 2-year insurance bar differs from the 60-day receivership-claims clock in Sec. 16(l) — different tracks, different courts.

citation: RA 3591, Sec. 22(e) (as amended by RA 11840; systemic-risk paragraphs retained)
verbatim:
(e) The Corporation is authorized to make loans to, or purchase the assets of, or assume liabilities of, or make deposits in:

(1) A bank in danger of closing, upon its acquisition by a qualified investor; or

(2) A qualified investor, upon its purchase of all assets and assumption of all liabilities of a bank in danger of closing; or

(3) A surviving or consolidated institution that has merged or consolidated with a bank in danger of closing; upon such terms and conditions as the Board of Directors may prescribe, when in the opinion of the Board of Directors, such acquisition, purchase of assets, assumption of liabilities, merger or consolidation, is essential to provide adequate banking service in the community or maintain financial stability in the economy.

The Corporation may, taking into consideration the peculiar characteristics of Islamic banks, formulate rules and regulations for the extension of financial assistance under this section.

The Corporation, prior to the exercise of the powers under this section, shall determine that actual payoff and liquidation thereof will be more expensive than the exercise of this power: Provided, That when the Monetary Board has determined that there are systemic consequences of a probable failure or closure of an insured bank, the Corporation may grant financial assistance to such insured bank in such amount as may be necessary to prevent its failure or closure and/or restore the insured bank to viable operations, under such terms and condition as may be deemed necessary by the Board of Directors, subject to concurrence by the Monetary Board and without additional cost to the DIF at the time of granting the financial assistance.

[...]

A systemic risk refers to the possibility that failure of one bank to settle net transactions with other banks will trigger a chain reaction, depriving other banks of funds leading to a general shutdown of normal clearing and settlement activity. Systemic risk also means the likelihood of a sudden, unexpected collapse of confidence in a significant portion of the banking or financial system with potentially large real economic effects. Finally, the Corporation may not use its authority under this subsection to purchase the voting or common stock of an insured bank but it can enter into and enforce agreements that it determines to be necessary to protect its financial interests: Provided, That the financial assistance may take the form of equity or quasi-equity of the insured bank as may be deemed necessary by the Board of Directors with concurrence by the Monetary Board: Provided, further, That the Corporation shall dispose of such equity as soon as practicable.
explanation: Financial assistance = rescue BEFORE closure. PDIC may lend to, buy assets of, assume liabilities of, or place deposits in: (1) a bank in danger of closing that a qualified investor acquires; (2) the qualified investor itself on a full P&A; or (3) the surviving entity after a merger — whenever the Board finds it essential for community banking service or financial stability. Two brakes: the LEAST-COST test (assistance must be cheaper than payoff-plus-liquidation) and the systemic track (on MB determination of systemic consequences, PDIC may fund prevention/restoration with MB concurrence and no added DIF cost at grant). The omitted rule: no buying the bank's voting/common stock — though equity or quasi-equity assistance is allowed if the Board, with MB concurrence, finds it necessary, to be disposed of as soon as practicable.

citation: RA 3591, Sec. 27 (as renumbered by RA 10846; text from RA 9302)
verbatim:
No court, except the Court of Appeals, shall issue any temporary restraining order, preliminary injunction or preliminary mandatory injunction against the Corporation for any action under this Act.

This prohibition shall apply in all cases, disputes or controversies instituted by a private party, the insured bank, or any shareholder of the insured bank.

The Supreme Court may issue a restraining order or injunction when the matter is of extreme urgency involving a constitutional issue, such that unless a temporary restraining order is issued, grave injustice and irreparable injury will arise. The party applying for the issuance of a restraining order or injunction shall file a bond in an amount to be fixed by the Supreme Court, which bond shall accrue in favor of the Corporation if the court should finally decide that the applicant was not entitled to the relief sought.

Any restraining order or injunction issued in violation of this Section is void and of no force and effect and any judge who has issued the same shall suffer the penalty of suspension of at least sixty (60) days without pay.
explanation: PDIC's shield against suit-based disruption. ONLY the Court of Appeals may enjoin PDIC actions under the charter — RTCs and all other courts cannot, whoever sues (depositor, bank, or shareholder). The lone exception: the Supreme Court itself, and only for extremely urgent CONSTITUTIONAL issues, with a bond favoring PDIC if the applicant loses. A void injunction exposes the issuing judge to at least 60 days suspension without pay. The Supreme Court invoked this shield in So v. PDIC and Chugani to keep deposit-insurance certiorari petitions in the CA. Remember: no TRO from the RTC against a PDIC takeover, payout, or claim denial — ever.

verbatim:
Section 11. When there is a failure of prompt corrective action as declared by the Monetary Board due to capital deficiency, the Corporation and the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas may examine, inquire or look into the deposit records of a bank: Provided, That such authority may not be exercised when the failure of prompt corrective action is due to grounds other than capital deficiency. For this purpose, banks, their officers and employees are hereby mandated to disclose and report to the Corporation and the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas or their duly authorized officers and employees, the required deposit account information.

The Corporation and the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, their duly authorized officers or employees are prohibited from disclosing information obtained under this section to any person, government official, bureau or office. Any act done pursuant to this section shall not be deemed as a violation of Republic Act No. 1405, as amended, Republic Act No. 6426, as amended, Republic Act No. 8791, and other similar laws protecting or safeguarding the secrecy or confidentiality of bank deposits. Any unauthorized disclosure of the information under this section shall be subject to the same penalty under the laws protecting the secrecy or confidentiality of bank deposits.
explanation: The distressed-bank examination power. Once the MB declares prompt-corrective-action failure DUE TO CAPITAL DEFICIENCY (and only then — other PCA grounds do not trigger it), PDIC and BSP may look into DEPOSIT RECORDS, and bank officers must disclose the required account information. The law expressly says this is NOT a violation of the deposit-secrecy laws (RA 1405, RA 6426, RA 8791) — a statutory exception — but anyone who leaks what they learn faces the same penalties as those secrecy laws impose. The omitted last sentence preserves the MB's other lawful actions. Links to Sec. 9(Eighth), which extends the same look-through to findings of fraud or unsafe/unsound banking.

citation: RA 3591, Sec. 8 (as amended by RA 11840; runoff paragraphs retained)
verbatim:
Section 8. (a) Whenever upon examination by the Corporation into the condition of any insured bank, it shall be disclosed that an insured bank or its directors or agents have committed, are committing or about to commit unsafe or unsound banking, or have violated, are violating or about to violate any provisions of any law or regulation to which the insured bank is subject. The Board of Directors shall submit the report of the examination to the Monetary Board.

(b) The Corporation may terminate the insured status of any bank that fails or refuses to comply, within thirty (30) days from notice, with any cease-and-desist order issued by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, pertaining to a deposit-related unsafe and/or unsound banking.

[...]

Such termination shall be final and executory, and shall be effective upon publication of the notice of termination in a newspaper of general circulation.

The deposits of each depositor in the bank on the effective date of the termination of insurance coverage, less all subsequent withdrawals, shall continue to be insured up to the maximum deposit insurance coverage for a period of one hundred eighty (180) days. Additions to, or renewal of, existing deposits and new deposits in such bank after the effective date of termination of insured status of the bank shall not be insured by the Corporation.

The bank shall not advertise or represent that additions to, or renewal of, existing deposits and new deposits made after the effective date of termination are covered by deposit insurance.
explanation: The co-regulation escalator. PDIC examines and REPORTS to the Monetary Board; the BSP issues the cease-and-desist order; if the bank defies it for 30 days on a deposit-related matter, PDIC may TERMINATE the bank's insured status. Termination is final and executory on publication — but existing depositors get a 180-DAY RUNOFF: balances as of termination day (less later withdrawals) stay insured up to the MDIC for 180 days, while new money after that date is uninsured, and the bank must not advertise otherwise (same rule restated in IRR Rule VII, Sec. 3). Note: the runoff paragraphs above are the RA 10846 Sec. 8(c) text retained through RA 11840; the online reproduction of the last sentence shows an evident typographical error ('aye' for 'are'), corrected here. Compare: termination of INSURED STATUS (bank keeps operating, uninsured) is different from closure (bank stops operating).

verbatim: It is hereby declared to be the policy of the Government to give encouragement to the people to deposit their money in banking institutions and to discourage private hoarding so that the same may be properly utilized by banks in authorized loans to assist in the economic development of the country.
explanation: The law exists to build trust in banks: people who are confident their deposits stay secret will deposit instead of hoarding cash at home, and banks can then lend those funds for economic development. For an accountancy student, this policy explains every rule that follows — confidentiality is the default because public confidence in the banking system is the State's goal. Quoted by the Supreme Court in garnishment and inquiry cases as the intent behind the secrecy rule.

verbatim: All deposits of whatever nature with banks or banking institutions in the Philippines including investments in bonds issued by the Government of the Philippines, its political subdivisions and its instrumentalities, are hereby considered as of an absolutely confidential nature and may not be examined, inquired or looked into by any person, government official, bureau or office, except upon written permission of the depositor, or in cases of impeachment, or upon order of a competent court in cases of bribery or dereliction of duty of public officials, or in cases where the money deposited or invested is the subject matter of the litigation.
explanation: This is the core of the module. Coverage has two limbs: (1) all deposits of whatever nature with Philippine banks or banking institutions — peso savings, checking, and time deposits, and the Supreme Court has applied the law to trust/SPAN accounts (Ejercito); and (2) investments in bonds issued by the Government, its political subdivisions, and instrumentalities. Confidentiality is 'absolute' against everyone — any person, government official, bureau, or office — subject to only four statutory exceptions: written permission of the depositor; impeachment; court order in bribery or dereliction-of-duty cases against public officials; and cases where the deposited money itself is the subject matter of the litigation. Later special laws add further inquiry pathways (AMLA, tax, PDIC, unclaimed balances), and jurisprudence allows garnishment of peso deposits (Ortega). Foreign currency deposits are no longer governed by this section — they follow RA 6426, Sec. 8 as amended by PD 1246.

verbatim: It shall be unlawful for any official or employee of a banking institution to disclose to any person other than those mentioned in Section two hereof any information concerning said deposits.
explanation: Section 2 states the confidentiality rule; Section 3 creates the criminally punishable act: disclosure by any official or employee of a banking institution to anyone outside the Section 2 exceptions. Note the persons covered — bank directors, officers, tellers, and staff — and the breadth of 'any information concerning said deposits' (balances, movements, and account existence alike). A bank employee who leaks a client's balance to a business rival, a spouse in a private dispute, or media violates this section. Lawful disclosure happens only through a Section 2 exception or a later special law.

verbatim: All Acts or parts of Acts, Special Charters, Executive Orders, Rules and Regulations which are inconsistent with the provisions of this Act are hereby repealed.
explanation: Standard repealing clause: any earlier law, charter, executive order, or regulation inconsistent with RA 1405 gives way to it. It confirms that bank-deposit confidentiality overrides older disclosure rules, though later special laws (AMLA, tax, PDIC charter) can and do carve out their own inquiry powers.

verbatim: Any violation of this law will subject offender upon conviction, to an imprisonment of not more than five years or a fine of not more than twenty thousand pesos or both, in the discretion of the court.
explanation: Penalty upon conviction: imprisonment of up to five years, a fine of up to twenty thousand pesos, or both, at the court's discretion. This punishes unlawful disclosure (Sec. 3) and any other violation of the Act. Compare with RA 6426, Sec. 10 (one to five years plus P5,000-P25,000 for willful violations) and the Unclaimed Balances Law's P500/month administrative penalty for reporting defaults.

verbatim: This Act shall take effect upon its approval.
explanation: Effectivity clause. RA 1405 was approved on September 9, 1955 and took effect immediately. The current text in force is the original 1955 text of Secs. 2-3, restored after PD 1792's amendments were repealed by RA 7653, Sec. 135.

verbatim: Except as may be provided for in Section 46 and 132 of this Act, Republic Act No. 265, as amended, the provisions of any other law, special charters, rule or regulation issued pursuant to said Republic Act No. 265, as amended, or parts thereof, which may be inconsistent with the provisions of this Act are hereby repealed. Presidential Decree No. 1792 is likewise repealed.
explanation: The key sentence for this module is the last one: PD 1792 is expressly repealed. PD 1792 (1981) had added two Sec. 2 exceptions — Monetary-Board-authorized examination on suspected bank fraud, and independent-auditor examination for bank audits. Its repeal in 1993 restored RA 1405's original four exceptions, which is the text the Supreme Court E-Library presents as current law. Exam trap: several Supreme Court decisions (Union Bank, Marquez, Ejercito) still reproduce the repealed PD 1792-era six-item enumeration — the controlling statutory text has only four exceptions, plus pathways created by later special laws.

citation: NIRC, Sec. 6(F), as amended by RA No. 10021, Sec. 3 (excerpt)
verbatim: (F) Authority of the Commissioner to Inquire into Bank Deposit Accounts and Other Related Information Held by Financial Institutions. - Notwithstanding any contrary provision of Republic Act No. 1405, Republic Act No. 6426, otherwise known as the Foreign Currency Deposit Act of the Philippines, and other general and special laws, the Commissioner is hereby authorized to inquire into the bank deposits and other related information held by financial institutions of: (1) A decedent to determine his gross estate. (2) Any taxpayer who has filed an application for compromise of his tax liability under Sec. 204 (A)(2) reason of financial incapacity to pay his tax liability. In case a taxpayer files an application to compromise the payment of his tax liabilities on his claim that his financial position demonstrates a clear inability to pay the tax assessed, his application shall not be considered unless and until he waives in writing his privilege under Republic Act No. 1405, Republic Act No. 6426, otherwise known as the Foreign Currency Deposit Act of the Philippines, or under other general or special laws, and such waiver shall constitute the authority of the Commissioner to inquire into the bank deposits of the taxpayer.
