(3) A specific taxpayer or taxpayers subject of a request for the supply of tax information from a foreign tax authority pursuant to an international convention or agreement on tax matters to which the Philippines is a signatory or a party of: Provided, That the information obtained from the banks and other financial institutions may be used by the Bureau of Internal Revenue for tax assessment, verification, audit and enforcement purposes.
explanation: Excerpt of Sec. 6(F): the Commissioner of Internal Revenue may inquire into bank deposits — expressly overriding both RA 1405 and RA 6426 — only through three paths: (1) a decedent's deposits, to determine the gross estate for estate-tax purposes; (2) a taxpayer who applied to compromise tax liability for financial incapacity, and only after the taxpayer waives secrecy in writing (without the waiver, the application is not even considered); (3) a specific taxpayer covered by a foreign tax authority's treaty-based information request, with the obtained information usable for BIR assessment, verification, audit, and enforcement. The subsection continues with request-form, foreseeable-relevance, transmittal, and confidentiality mechanics (summarized here). Practical upshot: in a routine audit of a living taxpayer, the BIR has no free-standing power to open deposit records — students should treat these three paths as exclusive.

sourceRefs.excerptHint: Inquiry paths, waiver rule, and use proviso (treaty-request mechanics summarized)

citation: RA No. 3591, Sec. 8, Eighth power, as amended by RA No. 11840, Sec. 7
verbatim: Eighth - To examine the records and books of accounts and require information and reports from depository institutions in case there is a finding of fraud or unsafe or unsound banking related to deposit-taking: Provided, That, notwithstanding the provisions of Republic Act No. 1405, as amended, Republic Act No. 6426, as amended, Republic Act No. 8791, and other laws, the Corporation and/or the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, may inquire into or examine deposit accounts and all information related thereto in case there is a finding of unsafe or unsound banking practice: Provided, further, That to avoid overlapping of efforts, the examination shall maximize the efficient use of the relevant reports, information, and findings of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, which it shall make available to the Corporation.
explanation: When there is a finding of unsafe or unsound banking practice, the PDIC and/or the BSP may inquire into or examine deposit accounts and related information — expressly overriding RA 1405, RA 6426, and RA 8791. This is the examination-related exception students often misattribute to a general BSP examination power: the trigger is a finding of fraud or unsafe/unsound deposit-taking, not routine supervision. (RA 11840 defines 'unsafe and unsound banking' by reference to BSP definitions under RA 7653.) The Supreme Court in PDIC v. Philippine Countryside Rural Bank separately held that PDIC's Sec. 9(b-1) investigation power needs no Monetary Board approval, unlike examination powers.

citation: Act No. 3936, Sec. 2, as amended by PD No. 679, Sec. 1 (excerpt)
verbatim: Immediately after the taking effect of this Act and within the month of January of every odd year, all banks, building and loan associations, and trust corporations shall forward to the Treasurer of the Philippines a statement, under oath, of their respective managing officers, of all credits and deposits held by them in favor of persons known to be dead, or who have not made further deposits or withdrawals during the preceding ten years or more, arranged in alphabetical order according to the names of creditors and depositors, and showing: (a) The names and last known place of residence or post office addresses of the persons in whose favor such unclaimed balances stand; (b) The amount and the date of the outstanding unclaimed balance and whether the same is in money or in security, and if the latter, the nature of the same; (c) The date when the person in whose favor the unclaimed balance stands died, if known, or the date when he made his last deposit or withdrawal; and (d) The interest due on such unclaimed balance, if any, and the amount thereof. A copy of the above sworn statement shall be posted in a conspicuous place in the premises of the bank, building and loan association, or trust corporation concerned for at least sixty days from the date of filing thereof: Provided, That immediately before filing the above sworn statement, the bank, building and loan association, and trust corporation shall communicate with the person in whose favor the unclaimed balance stands at his last known place of residence or post office address.
explanation: Excerpt stating the report-and-posting duties; Secs. 1 and 3-5 are taught alongside in lesson prose. 'Unclaimed balances' (Sec. 1) means credits or deposits — money, bullion, securities, or other evidence of indebtedness plus interest — favoring a person known to be dead or with no deposit or withdrawal for ten years or more; these are ultimately deposited with the Treasurer to government credit. Every odd-year January, banks must swear and file the detailed statement (names, addresses, amounts, dates, interest), first contact the depositor at the last known address, and post a copy conspicuously in the bank for at least 60 days. The Treasurer informs the Solicitor General, who files an escheat action joining the bank and the depositors (Sec. 3, with published summons and notice); failure to file the statement costs the bank P500 per month of default (Sec. 4); and a bank that duly turns over the balances is discharged from further liability (Sec. 5). This is a statutory disclosure pathway that overrides deposit confidentiality.

citation: RA No. 7653, Sec. 25, as amended by RA No. 11211, Sec. 8 (excerpt)
verbatim: The department heads and the examiners of the supervising and/or examining departments are hereby authorized to administer oaths to any director, officer, or employee of any institution under their respective supervision or subject to their examination, and to compel the presentation of all books, documents, papers or records necessary in their judgment to ascertain the facts relative to the true condition of any institution as well as the books and records of persons and entities relative to or in connection with the operations, activities or transactions of the institution under examination, subject to the provision of existing laws protecting or safeguarding the secrecy or confidentiality of bank deposits as well as investments of private persons, natural or juridical, in debt instruments issued by the Government.
explanation: Excerpt of the BSP examination power — read the tail clause carefully: the power to compel books and records is expressly 'subject to' secrecy laws. There is therefore no general BSP-examination exception to RA 1405; since PD 1792's repeal, examiners must respect deposit confidentiality during regular or special examinations. Lawful examination-related inquiry into deposits runs instead through the PDIC Charter's Eighth power (finding of fraud or unsafe/unsound deposit-taking) or a depositor's own waiver, such as the DOSRI waiver in Sec. 26. A classic exam trap is to list 'BSP examination' as a blanket exception — it is not.

sourceRefs.excerptHint: Examination power subject to secrecy laws (excerpt)

verbatim: Any director, officer or stockholder who, together with his related interest, contracts a loan or any form of financial accommodation from: (1) his bank; or (2) from a bank (a) which is a subsidiary of a bank holding company of which both his bank and the lending bank are subsidiaries or (b) in which a controlling proportion of the shares is owned by the same interest that owns a controlling proportion of the shares of his bank, in excess of five percent (5%) of the capital and surplus of the bank, or in the maximum amount permitted by law, whichever is lower, shall be required by the lending bank to waive the secrecy of his deposits of whatever nature in all banks in the Philippines. Any information obtained from an examination of his deposits shall be held strictly confidential and may be used by the examiners only in connection with their supervisory and examination responsibility or by the Bangko Sentral in an appropriate legal action it has initiated involving the deposit account.
explanation: The DOSRI (directors, officers, stockholders, and related interests) waiver: a bank insider borrowing above the statutory threshold from his own or a related bank must waive secrecy over deposits of whatever nature in all Philippine banks. It is a consent-based pathway — the insider's written waiver functions like the depositor's written permission under RA 1405, Sec. 2 — but the law strictly limits use of what examiners learn (supervisory purposes or a BSP-initiated legal action on the account). Unamended by RA 11211; still cited in current bank loan-waiver forms.

verbatim: This Act shall be known as the "Foreign Currency Deposit Act of the Philippines."
explanation: Short title. RA 6426 (approved April 4, 1972) institutes the foreign currency deposit system: Philippine banks in good standing, designated by the Central Bank (now BSP), accept deposits in foreign currencies that form part of the international reserve. Its secrecy regime now sits in Sec. 8 as amended by PD 1246 — stricter than RA 1405, with only the depositor's written permission as an internal exception and an express bar on attachment and garnishment.

verbatim: Any person, natural or juridical, may, in accordance with the provisions of this Act, deposit with such Philippine banks in good standing, as may, upon application, be designated by the Central Bank for the purpose, foreign currencies which are acceptable as part of the international reserve, except those which are required by the Central Bank to be surrendered in accordance with the provisions of Republic Act Numbered Two hundred sixty-five.
explanation: Who may open a foreign currency deposit, and where: any natural or juridical person — individuals and companies alike, residents and non-residents — may deposit eligible foreign currencies (those acceptable as international reserve) with designated banks in good standing. The 'Central Bank' designation role now belongs to the BSP. For commerce students: an exporter holding dollars or a BPO receiving foreign remittances can lawfully keep those funds in the Philippine banking system under this Act, enjoying its confidentiality, withdrawability, and tax features.

verbatim: The banks designated by the Central Bank under Section two hereof shall have the authority: (1) To accept deposits and to accept foreign currencies in trust: Provided, That numbered accounts for recording and servicing of said deposits shall be allowed; (2) To issue certificates to evidence such deposits; (3) To discount said certificates; (4) To accept said deposits as collateral for loans subject to such rules and regulations as may be promulgated by the Central Bank from time to time; and (5) To pay interest in foreign currency on such deposits.
explanation: What designated banks may do with foreign currency deposits: accept them (including in trust), allow numbered accounts, issue and discount deposit certificates, take the deposits as loan collateral, and pay interest in foreign currency. The numbered-accounts proviso is itself a confidentiality feature — the account is serviced by number rather than name. Note that using the deposit as loan collateral is voluntary dealing by the depositor, not an exception that lets outsiders pry into the account.

verbatim: There shall be no restriction on the withdrawal by the depositor of his deposit or on the transferability of the same abroad except those arising from the contract between the depositor and the bank.
explanation: Free withdrawability and transferability abroad: the State imposes no restriction — only the depositor's own contract with the bank can limit withdrawal or outward transfer. Together with confidentiality (Sec. 8) and tax exemption (Sec. 6), this was the incentive package that drew foreign currency into Philippine banks. Do not confuse this freedom of the depositor with freedom of outsiders: creditors and investigators remain barred by Sec. 8.

citation: RA No. 6426, Sec. 6, as amended by PD No. 1246, Sec. 1
verbatim: All foreign currency deposits made under this Act, as amended by Presidential Decree No. 1035, as well as foreign currency deposits authorized under Presidential Decree No. 1034, including interest and all other income or earnings of such deposits, are hereby exempted from any and all taxes whatsoever irrespective of whether or not these deposits are made by residents or non-residents so long as the deposits are eligible or allowed under aforementioned laws and, in the case of non-residents, irrespective of whether or not they are engaged in trade or business in the Philippines.
explanation: PD 1246 replaced the original Sec. 6 (which exempted only interest earned by non-residents not in business) with a blanket exemption: eligible foreign currency deposits plus all interest and earnings are exempt from any and all taxes, whether the depositor is resident or non-resident. Tax is not this module's focus, but the exemption completes the FCD incentive picture (confidentiality + withdrawability + tax exemption) and explains why the system — and its secrecy — is jealously guarded. Eligibility under the Act and its regulations remains a condition.

citation: RA No. 6426, Sec. 8, as amended by PD No. 1246, Sec. 2
verbatim: All foreign currency deposits authorized under this Act, as amended by Presidential Decree No. 1035, as well as foreign currency deposits authorized under Presidential Decree No. 1034, are hereby declared as and considered of an absolutely confidential nature and, except upon the written permission of the depositor, in no instance shall such foreign currency deposits be examined, inquired or looked into by any person, government official, bureau or office whether judicial or administrative or legislative or any other entity whether public or private: Provided, however, that said foreign currency deposits shall be exempt from attachment, garnishment, or any other order or process of any court, legislative body, government agency or any administrative body whatsoever.
explanation: The heart of foreign currency secrecy, and deliberately stricter than RA 1405: the only internal exception is the depositor's written permission — there is no impeachment, bribery/dereliction, or subject-matter-of-litigation exception — and the deposits are expressly exempt from attachment, garnishment, or any other court, legislative, or administrative process. History: the original Sec. 8 (1972) made FCD secrecy follow RA 1405; PD 1035 (1976) kept that while adding usury/uniform-currency non-applicability; PD 1246 (1977) imposed this absolute regime to attract inflows. Coverage reaches both RA 6426/PD 1035 deposits and offshore-banking (PD 1034) deposits. Two cautions: (1) Salvacion v. Central Bank refused to apply the garnishment exemption on peculiar equitable facts — a narrow ruling, not a general license; (2) later 'notwithstanding RA 6426' laws (AMLA Sec. 11, NIRC Sec. 6(F), PDIC Charter Sec. 8) reach foreign currency deposits through their own procedures, a textual tension with Sec. 12-A that the Supreme Court has not squarely resolved.

sourceRefs.excerptHint: Court's quotation confirming the Sec. 8 reading

verbatim: The deposits under this Act shall be insured under the provisions of Republic Act Numbered Three thousand five hundred ninety-one, as amended, as well as its implementing rules and regulations: Provided, That insurance payment shall be in the same currency in which the insured deposits are denominated.
explanation: Foreign currency deposits are PDIC-insured like peso deposits, but any insurance payout is made in the same currency as the deposit (dollars for dollar deposits). This links the module to PDIC insurance: the same confidentiality that shields the account during the bank's life does not prevent the insurance system from working if the bank closes. Full PDIC treatment belongs to the PDIC module.

verbatim: Any willful violation of this Act or any regulation duly promulgated by the Monetary Board pursuant hereto shall subject the offender upon conviction to an imprisonment of not less than one year nor more than five years or a fine of not less than five thousand pesos nor more than twenty-five thousand pesos, or both such fine and imprisonment at the discretion of the court.
explanation: Penalties for willful violation of RA 6426 or its Monetary Board regulations: one to five years' imprisonment, a P5,000-P25,000 fine, or both. Note 'willful' — the violation must be deliberate — and that the ranges have both floors and ceilings, unlike RA 1405's ceilings-only penalty (up to five years and/or up to P20,000).

citation: RA No. 6426, Sec. 12-A, as added by PD No. 1246, Sec. 3
verbatim: In the event a new enactment or regulation is issued decreasing the rights hereunder granted, such new enactment or regulation shall not apply to foreign currency deposits already made or existing at the time of issuance of such new enactment or regulation, but such new enactment or regulation shall apply only to foreign currency deposits made after its issuance.
explanation: Vested-rights protection: a later law or regulation that decreases FCD depositor rights applies only prospectively, to deposits made after its issuance — existing deposits keep the old rights. (Sec. 7 carries the same idea for Central Bank regulations.) Students should flag, not resolve, the tension between this section and later 'notwithstanding RA 6426' inquiry statutes (AMLA, tax, PDIC): the standard teaching is that those statutes' express override reaches foreign currency deposits through their own procedures, and no Supreme Court decision squarely applies Sec. 12-A to block them. State both texts on an exam and note the point as unsettled.

verbatim: This Act shall be known as the "Truth in Lending Act."
explanation: The short title of the law. When an exam problem says 'Truth in Lending Act' or 'TILA,' it means RA 3765, the 1963 law that forces creditors to disclose the true cost of credit before the borrower commits.

verbatim: Declaration of Policy. It is hereby declared to be the policy of the State to protect its citizens from a lack of awareness of the true cost of credit to the user by assuring a full disclosure of such cost with a view of preventing the uninformed use of credit to the detriment of the national economy.
explanation: The State's goal is borrower awareness: every user of credit must know the TRUE cost of borrowing before deciding. The Supreme Court explains that banks can conceal true cost through hidden charges, uncertainty of interest rates, and deductions from the loaned amount — disclosure lets the debtor give full consent and properly evaluate options. For accountants, this is the legal backbone of loan disclosure statements and effective-rate computations.

sourceRefs.section: Liability for Violation of Truth in Lending Act

verbatim: (1) "Board" means the Monetary Board of the Central Bank of the Philippines.
explanation: 'Board' is the Monetary Board — the body that issues the implementing rules (today acting for the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, e.g. BSP Circular No. 730). Remember: disclosure duties are read 'in accordance with rules and regulations prescribed by the Board,' so the statute and BSP rules work together.

verbatim: (2) "Credit" means any loan, mortgage, deed of trust, advance, or discount; any conditional sales contract; any contract to sell, or sale or contract of sale of property or services, either for present or future delivery, under which part or all of the price is payable subsequent to the making of such sale or contract; any rental-purchase contract; any contract or arrangement for the hire, bailment, or leasing of property; any option, demand, lien, pledge, or other claim against, or for the delivery of, property or money; any purchase, or other acquisition of, or any credit upon the security of, any obligation of claim arising out of any of the foregoing; and any transaction or series of transactions having a similar purpose or effect.
explanation: 'Credit' is deliberately broad: any arrangement where payment comes AFTER the transaction — loans, mortgages, installment sales of goods or services, leases, pledges, and anything with a similar purpose or effect. Exam point: an installment sale of a laptop or a car lease can be 'credit' under TILA, not just bank loans. The catch-all phrase ('similar purpose or effect') prevents creditors from relabeling a credit deal to escape disclosure.

verbatim: (3) "Finance charge" includes interest, fees, service charges, discounts, and such other charges incident to the extension of credit as the Board may be regulation prescribe.
explanation: 'Finance charge' covers every cost of borrowing: interest, fees, service charges, discounts, plus any other charge incident to the extension of credit that the Board prescribes by regulation. Note the word 'includes' — the list is open, not closed. (The phrase 'may be regulation prescribe' is a [sic] in the statutory text, read as 'may by regulation prescribe'.) Accounting relevance: this is the population of costs that must appear in the disclosure statement and feed the effective interest rate.

verbatim: (4) "Creditor" means any person engaged in the business of extending credit (including any person who as a regular business practice make loans or sells or rents property or services on a time, credit, or installment basis, either as principal or as agent) who requires as an incident to the extension of credit, the payment of a finance charge.
explanation: A 'creditor' has TWO requisites: (1) engaged in the BUSINESS of extending credit (lenders, installment sellers, lessors acting as principal or agent — as a regular practice), AND (2) requires payment of a finance charge as an incident of the credit. Both must concur. A neighbor who lends once for free is not a creditor; a bank, financing company, or appliance store selling on installment with interest is. (The singular verb 'make' is a [sic] in the statutory text.)

verbatim: (5) "Person" means any individual, corporation, partnership, association, or other organized group of persons, or the legal successor or representative of the foregoing, and includes the Philippine Government or any agency thereof, or any other government, or of any of its political subdivisions, or any agency of the foregoing.
explanation: 'Person' covers natural and juridical persons, successors and representatives — and even the government and its agencies. So a government credit program can extend 'credit' to a 'person,' although Sec. 6(d) later exempts the government from the Act's punishments and penalties.

verbatim: Any creditor shall furnish to each person to whom credit is extended, prior to the consummation of the transaction, a clear statement in writing setting forth, to the extent applicable and in accordance with rules and regulations prescribed by the Board, the following information: (1) the cash price or delivered price of the property or service to be acquired; (2) the amounts, if any, to be credited as down payment and/or trade-in; (3) the difference between the amounts set forth under clauses (1) and (2); (4) the charges, individually itemized, which are paid or to be paid by such person in connection with the transaction but which are not incident to the extension of credit; (5) the total amount to be financed; (6) the finance charge expressed in terms of pesos and centavos; and (7) the percentage that the finance bears to the total amount to be financed expressed as a simple annual rate on the outstanding unpaid balance of the obligation.
explanation: The heart of TILA. Every creditor must give every borrower, BEFORE the deal is consummated, a clear WRITTEN statement showing: cash price, down payment/trade-in, the difference, itemized non-credit charges, total amount financed, the finance charge in pesos and centavos, and the finance charge as a simple annual rate on the outstanding balance. 'To the extent applicable' means the creditor discloses what fits the transaction. Exam anchors from jurisprudence: disclosure AFTER execution is not substantial compliance (Beluso); charges missing from the disclosure statement cannot be collected even if the promissory note stipulates them (Sampaguita).

sourceRefs.section: Liability for Violation of Truth in Lending Act
sourceRefs.excerptHint: prior to consummation, not substantial compliance
no right to collect undisclosed charges

verbatim: The Board shall prescribe such rules and regulations as may be necessary or proper in carrying out the provisions of this Act. Any rule or regulation prescribed hereunder may contain such classifications and differentiations as in the judgment of the Board are necessary or proper to effectuate the purposes of this Act or to prevent circumvention or evasion, or to facilitate the enforcement of this Act, or any rule or regulation issued thereunder.
explanation: Sec. 5 is the rulemaking grant: the Monetary Board fleshes out the Act and may classify or differentiate transactions to achieve its purpose, stop circumvention or evasion, and ease enforcement. This is the statutory basis of the BSP disclosure rules in the MORB (X307) and BSP Circular No. 730. For the exam, pair Sec. 5 with Sec. 4: the 'clear statement in writing' is given 'in accordance with rules and regulations prescribed by the Board.'

sourceRefs.excerptHint: MORB amendments under MB Resolution No. 1018

verbatim: (a) Any creditor who in connection with any credit transaction fails to disclose to any person any information in violation of this Act or any regulation issued thereunder shall be liable to such person in the amount of P100 or in an amount equal to twice the finance charged required by such creditor in connection with such transaction, whichever is the greater, except that such liability shall not exceed P2,000 on any credit transaction. Action to recover such penalty may be brought by such person within one year from the date of the occurrence of the violation, in any court of competent jurisdiction. In any action under this subsection in which any person is entitled to a recovery, the creditor shall be liable for reasonable attorney's fees and court costs as determined by the court.
explanation: The CIVIL liability for nondisclosure. Formula: the borrower recovers P100 OR twice the finance charge required — whichever is GREATER — capped at P2,000 per credit transaction, plus reasonable attorney's fees and court costs. Prescription: 1 year from the violation, filed in any court of competent jurisdiction. Beluso teaches: (1) this civil action may be brought separately and independently of any criminal case (and may be joined with other actions); (2) the cause of action accrues only when the finance charge is required — in Beluso, on the 2 September 1998 demand, so the 9 February 1999 filing was timely; (3) the Court sustained a P26,000 penalty recovery (P2,000 cap applied across the transactions).

sourceRefs.section: Liability for Violation of Truth in Lending Act

verbatim: (b) Except as specified in subsection (a) of this section, nothing contained in this Act or any regulation contained in this Act or any regulation thereunder shall affect the validity or enforceability of any contract or transactions.
explanation: Nondisclosure does NOT void the contract. Except for the Sec. 6(a) civil penalty, the Act leaves the validity and enforceability of the contract or transaction untouched — the borrower still owes the obligation (though undisclosed charges themselves cannot be collected, per Sampaguita). Classic exam trap: TILA violation = penalty and unenforceability of hidden charges, not nullity of the whole loan. (The doubled phrase 'any regulation contained in this Act or any regulation thereunder' is a [sic] in the statutory text.)

verbatim: (c) Any person who willfully violates any provision of this Act or any regulation issued thereunder shall be fined by not less than P1,00 or more than P5,000 or imprisonment for not less than 6 months, nor more than one year or both.
explanation: The CRIMINAL liability: a WILLFUL violation is punished by fine (floor to ceiling), imprisonment of 6 months to 1 year, or both. Two exam-critical notes: (1) criminal liability requires willfulness, unlike the Sec. 6(a) civil penalty; (2) the fine floor reads 'P1,00' [sic] in every statute reproduction — the Supreme Court itself, quoting this paragraph in UCPB v. Beluso, reads it as P1,000. Quote the [sic] honestly and cite the Court's reading.

sourceRefs.section: Liability for Violation of Truth in Lending Act

verbatim: (d) No punishment or penalty provided by this Act shall apply to the Philippine Government or any agency or any political subdivision thereof.
explanation: The government is exempt from the Act's punishments and penalties. Pair with Sec. 3(5): the government can be a 'person' extending credit, but no Sec. 6 punishment or penalty applies to it or its agencies and political subdivisions.

verbatim: (e) A final judgment hereafter rendered in any criminal proceeding under this Act to the effect that a defendant has willfully violated this Act shall be prima facie evidence against such defendant in an action or proceeding brought by any other party against such defendant under this Act as to all matters respecting which said judgment would be an estoppel as between the parties thereto.
explanation: A final criminal conviction for willful violation becomes PRIMA FACIE evidence against the same defendant in a later action by any other party under the Act — but only as to matters where the judgment would be an estoppel between the parties. In plain terms: once willfulness is criminally established, a subsequent civil claimant starts with a presumption in their favor on the overlapping issues. 'Prima facie' means rebuttable, not conclusive.

verbatim: This Act shall become effective upon approval.
explanation: The Act took effect upon approval — 22 June 1963. There is no statute-level amendment on record; the disclosure regime has since been elaborated through BSP regulation, notably BSP Circular No. 730 (effective 1 July 2012).

verbatim: [Excerpt] As a general rule, loan terms shall be disclosed to all types of borrower. For small business/retail/consumer credit, the following are the minimum information to be disclosed (sample form in Appendix 19): 1. The total amount to be financed; 2. The finance charges expressed in terms of pesos and centavos; 3. The net proceeds of the loan; and 4. The percentage that the finance charge bears to the total amount to be financed expressed as a simple annual rate or an effective annual interest rate (EIR) as described in item h of Subsection X307.1. EIR may also be quoted as a monthly rate in parallel with the quotation of the contractual rate. Banks are required to furnish each borrower a copy of the disclosure statement, prior to the consummation of the transaction.
explanation: The BSP's minimum disclosure checklist for small business, retail, and consumer credit: amount financed, finance charges in pesos and centavos, NET PROCEEDS of the loan, and the rate as a simple annual rate OR the effective interest rate (EIR). General rule: loan terms are disclosed to ALL borrower types. And the timing rule is explicit: the borrower gets a copy of the disclosure statement BEFORE consummation — the same timing the Supreme Court enforces in Beluso.

verbatim: [Excerpt] g. Finance charge includes interest, fees, service charges, discounts, and such other charges incident to the extension of credit. h. Simple annual rate is the uniform percentage which represents the ratio between the finance charge and the amount to be financed under the assumption that the loan is payable in one year with single payment upon maturity and there are no up-front deductions to principal. For loans with terms different from the above assumptions, the effective annual interest (EIR) rate shall be calculated and disclosed to the borrower as the relevant true cost of the loan comparable to the concept of simple annual rate. For loans with contractual interest rates stated on monthly basis, the effective interest rate may be expressed as a monthly rate. In accordance with the Philippine Accounting Standards (PAS) definition effective interest rate is the rate that exactly discounts estimated future cash flows through the life of the loan to the net amount of loan proceeds.
explanation: Two key BSP definitions. The 'simple annual rate' assumes a one-year, single-payment loan with no up-front deductions — a clean benchmark. For real-world loans (installments, deductions), the EIR must be computed and disclosed instead, and the EIR follows the PAS (accounting-standards) definition: the rate that exactly discounts estimated future cash flows over the loan's life to the net loan proceeds. This is where accountancy directly meets TILA: EIR is the time-value-of-money internal rate of the loan.

sourceRefs.excerptHint: finance charge, simple annual rate, EIR

verbatim: [Excerpt] Banks may only charge interest based on the outstanding balance of a loan at the beginning of an interest period. For a loan where principal is payable in installments, interest per installment period shall be calculated based on the outstanding balance of the loan at the beginning of each installment period. Towards this end, all loan-related documents shall show repayment schedules in a manner consistent with this provision. Marketing materials and presentations shall likewise be consistent with this provision.
explanation: Banks may charge interest ONLY on the outstanding balance at the start of each interest (or installment) period — no interest on amounts already repaid. Loan documents must show repayment schedules consistent with this, and even marketing materials must match. Practical effect: this kills add-on/flat-rate presentations that understate the true cost — the exact evil Sec. 2 of RA 3765 targets.

verbatim: [Excerpt] Banks shall post in conspicuous places in their principal place of business and branches, the information as contained in the revised format of disclosure statement (Appendix 19), with further enhancement through the Memorandum to All Banks to be issued for the purpose. The posters shall include an explicit notification that the disclosure statement is a required attachment to the loan contract and the customer has a right to demand a copy of such disclosure.
explanation: Beyond per-borrower disclosure, banks must POST the disclosure-statement information conspicuously in their offices and branches — with an explicit notice that the disclosure statement is a required attachment to the loan contract and that the customer has the right to demand a copy. Remember: disclosure is the borrower's RIGHT, not a bank courtesy.

sourceRefs.excerptHint: posters and right to demand a copy

verbatim: Employer — Any person, natural or juridical, domestic or foreign, who carries on in the Philippines any trade, business, industry, undertaking, or activity of any kind and uses the services of another person who is under his orders as regards the employment, except the government and any of its political subdivisions, branches or instrumentalities, including corporations owned or controlled by the Government: Provided, That a self-employed person shall be both employee and employer at the same time.
explanation: An employer is anyone running any trade or activity in the Philippines who uses another person's services under his orders. The government and its branches, subdivisions, instrumentalities, and GOCCs are excluded (their workers fall under the GSIS, not the SSS). The proviso matters for payroll thinking: a self-employed person wears both hats, so he shoulders both the employer and employee shares of the contribution. Remember: coverage follows the employment relationship — no employer-employee relationship, no compulsory coverage as employee (see Sec. 8(j)(1) and Gapayao v. Fulo).

verbatim: Employee — Any person who performs services for an employer in which either or both mental or physical efforts are used and who receives compensation for such services, where there is an employer-employee relationship: Provided, That a self-employed person shall be both employee and employer at the same time.
explanation: An employee is one who renders service (mental or physical) for compensation within an employer-employee relationship. For accountancy students: when classifying workers for SSS payroll compliance, apply the labor-law control test — the person for whom services are performed must have the right to control both the end and the manner and means (Gapayao). Job title, pakyaw/piece-rate pay, or irregular hours do not by themselves defeat employee status. Remember: a self-employed person is deemed both employee and employer, so he pays both shares.

verbatim: Employment — Any service performed by an employee for his employer except: (1) Services where there is no employer-employee relationship in accordance with existing labor laws, rules, regulations and jurisprudence; (2) Service performed in the employ of the Philippine Government or instrumentality or agency thereof; (3) Service performed in the employ of a foreign government or international organization, or their wholly-owned instrumentality: Provided, however, That this exemption notwithstanding, any foreign government, international organization or their wholly-owned instrumentality employing workers in the Philippines or employing Filipinos outside of the Philippines, may enter into an agreement with the Philippine Government for the inclusion of such employees in the SSS except those already covered by their respective civil service retirement systems: Provided, further, That the terms of such agreement shall conform with the provisions of this Act on coverage and amount of payment of contributions and benefits: Provided, finally, That the provisions of this Act shall be supplementary to any such agreement; and (4) Such other services performed by temporary and other employees which may be excluded by regulation of the Commission. Employees of bona fide independent contractors shall not be deemed employees of the employer engaging the service of said contractors.
explanation: Employment means covered service, minus four exclusions: (1) no employer-employee relationship (genuine independent contractors are out — but their own employees are covered as employees of the contractor); (2) Philippine government service (GSIS territory); (3) foreign government/international-organization service, unless brought in by agreement; (4) services the Commission excludes by regulation. Practical application: before enrolling a worker, HR/payroll must first settle whether he is an employee or a bona fide contractor's employee. Exam point: memorize the four exclusions — questions often test whether a government worker, a contractor's crew, or an embassy hire is compulsorily covered.

verbatim: Member — The worker who is covered under Section 9, Section 9-A and Section 9-B of this Act.
explanation: A member is simply a worker covered under any of the three coverage sections: employees (Sec. 9), self-employed (Sec. 9-A), and OFWs (Sec. 9-B). Every benefit provision that says 'a member' presupposes this status. Remember: voluntary members (non-working spouses, separated members who continue paying, permanent migrants) keep member status through continued coverage, not through a separate definition.

verbatim: Self-employed — Any person whose income is not derived from employment, as defined under this Act, as well as those workers enumerated in Section 9-A hereof.
explanation: Self-employed captures everyone whose income does not come from employment, plus the enumerated workers in Sec. 9-A (professionals, single proprietors and partners, actors/directors/scriptwriters/correspondents who are not employees, athletes/coaches/trainers/jockeys, farmers and fishermen). For compliance: these members register themselves, declare their monthly earnings, and pay both shares. Exam point: 'income not derived from employment' is the general test; the Sec. 9-A enumeration is expressly non-exclusive ('including, but not limited to').

verbatim: (a) Coverage in the SSS shall be compulsory upon all employees including kasambahays or domestic workers not over sixty (60) years of age and their employers: Provided, That any benefit already earned by the employees under private benefit plans existing at the time of the approval of this Act shall not be discontinued, reduced or otherwise impaired: Provided, further, That private plans which are existing and in force at the time of compulsory coverage shall be integrated with the plan of the SSS in such a way where the employer's contribution to his private plan is more than that required of him in this Act, he shall pay to the SSS only the contribution required of him and he shall continue his contribution to such private plan less his contribution to the SSS so that the employer's total contribution to his benefit plan and to the SSS shall be the same as his contribution to his private benefit plan before the compulsory coverage: Provided, further, That any changes, adjustments, modifications, eliminations or improvements in the benefits to be available under the remaining private plan, which may be necessary to adopt by reason of the reduced contributions thereto as a result of the integration, shall be subject to agreements between the employers and employees concerned: Provided, further, That the private benefit plan which the employer shall continue for his employees shall remain under the employer's management and control unless there is an existing agreement to the contrary: Provided, finally, That nothing in this Act shall be construed as a limitation on the right of employers and employees to agree on and adopt benefits which are over and above those provided under this Act. (b) Spouses who devote full time to managing the household and family affairs, unless they are also engaged in other vocation or employment which is subject to mandatory coverage, may be covered by the SSS on a voluntary basis.
explanation: Paragraph (a) states the core compulsory-coverage rule: every employee not over 60 — expressly including kasambahays and domestic workers — plus their employers. The provisos protect existing private plans: earned benefits cannot be cut, employer contributions integrate (SSS first, the balance stays with the private plan, total cost unchanged), adjustments need employer-employee agreement, and parties may always agree on benefits above the SSS floor. Paragraph (b) creates the non-working-spouse voluntary track: full-time homemakers may join voluntarily, unless they are already mandatorily covered by other work. Practical application: household employers must register kasambahays (current schedule: SSS Circular No. 2024-007, eff. 1 Jan 2025); payroll officers must never treat a private retirement plan as a substitute for SSS coverage. Remember: 'not over 60' is the age ceiling for compulsory employee coverage.

verbatim: Compulsory Coverage of the Self-Employed. — Coverage in the SSS shall also be compulsory upon such self-employed persons as may be determined by the Commission under such rules and regulations as it may prescribe, including, but not limited to the following: (a) All self-employed professionals; (b) Partners and single proprietors of businesses; (c) Actors and actresses, directors, scriptwriters and news correspondents who do not fall within the definition of the term 'employee' in Section 8(d) of this Act; (d) Professional athletes, coaches, trainers and jockeys; and (e) Individual farmers and fishermen. Unless otherwise specified herein, all provisions of this Act applicable to covered employees shall also be applicable to the covered self-employed persons.
explanation: Self-employed coverage is compulsory, not optional — the Commission only fills in the mechanics. The enumeration (professionals, partners and single proprietors, listed media/sports workers who are not employees, individual farmers and fishermen) is expressly non-exhaustive. The closing sentence is the workhorse: everything applicable to covered employees applies to covered self-employed persons unless the Act says otherwise. Practical application: a CPA in independent practice, a sari-sari store owner, and a tricycle operator are all compulsorily covered and pay both shares on declared earnings. Remember: freelancers who ARE employees of a client (control test) fall under Sec. 9, not Sec. 9-A.

verbatim: Compulsory Coverage of Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) — (a) Coverage in the SSS shall be compulsory upon all sea-based and land-based OFWs as defined under Republic Act No. 8042, otherwise known as the Migrant Workers and Overseas Filipinos Act of 1995, as amended by Republic Act No. 10022: Provided, That they are not over sixty (60) years of age. All benefit provisions under this Act shall apply to all covered OFWs. The benefits include, among others, retirement, death, disability, funeral, sickness and maternity. (b) Manning agencies are agents of their principals and are considered as employers of sea-based OFWs. For purposes of the implementation of this Act, any law to the contrary notwithstanding manning agencies are jointly and severally or solidarity liable with their principals with respect to the civil liabilities incurred for any violation of this Act. The persons having direct control, management or direction of the manning agencies shall be held criminally liable for any act or omission penalized under this Act notwithstanding Section 28(f) hereof. (c) Land-based OFWs are compulsory members of the SSS and considered in the same manner as self-employed persons under such rules and regulations that the Commission shall prescribe. (d) The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) and all its agencies involved in deploying OFWs for employment abroad are mandated to negotiate bilateral labor agreements with the OFWs' host countries to ensure that the employers of land-based OFWs, similar to the principals of sea-based OFWs, pay the required SSS contributions, in which case these land-based OFWs shall no longer be considered in the same manner as self-employed persons in this Act. Instead, they shall be considered as compulsorily covered employees with employer and employee shares in contributions that shall be provided for in the bilateral labor agreements and their implementing administrative agreements: Provided, That in countries which already extend social security coverage to OFWs, the DFA through the Philippine embassies and the DOLE shall negotiate further agreements to serve the best interests of the OFWs. (e) The DFA, the DOLE and the SSS shall ensure compulsory coverage of OFWs through bilateral social security and labor agreements and other measures for enforcement. (f) Upon the termination of their employment overseas, OFWs may continue to pay contributions on a voluntary basis to maintain their rights to full benefits. (g) Filipino permanent migrants, including Filipino immigrants, permanent residents and naturalized citizens of their host countries may be covered by the SSS on a voluntary basis.
explanation: RA 11199 made OFW coverage compulsory — the single biggest coverage expansion of the 2018 rewrite. Sea-based OFWs are treated as employees of their manning agencies, which are solidarily liable with foreign principals for civil liabilities, while the agency's controlling persons face criminal liability. Land-based OFWs are currently treated as self-employed (minimum MSC P8,000 under current SSS rules) until bilateral agreements shift their foreign employers into the employer-share role. Paragraphs (f) and (g) create two voluntary tracks: separated OFWs who keep paying, and permanent migrants. Practical application: manning agencies must remit like any employer; a land-based OFW budgets for both shares. Exam points: (1) OFW age ceiling is also 'not over 60'; (2) manning-agency solidary liability; (3) land-based OFW = self-employed treatment is the default rule, bilateral-agreement employee treatment the exception.

verbatim: Effective Date of Coverage. — Compulsory coverage of the employer shall take effect on the first day of his operation and that of the employee on the day of his employment: Provided, That the compulsory coverage of the self-employed person shall take effect upon his registration with the SSS.
explanation: Three effectivity triggers: the employer is covered from the first day of business operations; the employee from day one of employment (no probation or regularization requirement); the self-employed person only upon registration with the SSS. Practical application: a newly hired employee is already covered on his first day of work, so payroll must deduct from the first payroll period, and the employer must report him immediately (Sec. 24(a)) — delay risks damages if a contingency strikes. Remember the triplet: operation / employment / registration.

verbatim: Effect of Separation from Employment. — When an employee under compulsory coverage is separated from employment, his employer's contribution on his account and his obligation to pay contributions arising from that employment shall cease at the end of the month of separation, but said employee shall be credited with all contributions paid on his behalf and entitled to benefits according to the provisions of this Act. He may, however, continue to pay the total contributions to maintain his right to full benefit.
explanation: Separation ends the contribution obligation at the end of the month of separation — but never wipes the slate: all paid contributions stay credited and benefit rights survive. The separated employee may keep paying the total contribution (both shares) as a voluntary member to preserve full benefit rights. Practical application: resigned or retired employees deciding whether to continue paying should weigh the qualifying-contribution thresholds (120 for retirement pension, 36 for death/disability pension, 3 for sickness/maternity) against the voluntary cost. Remember: 'credited with all contributions' — SSS membership has no forfeiture of paid contributions.

verbatim: Effect of Interruption of Business or Professional Income. — If the self-employed member realizes no income in any given month, he shall not be required to pay contributions for that month. He may, however, be allowed to continue paying contributions under the same rules and regulations applicable to a separated employee member: Provided, That no retroactive payment of contributions shall be allowed other than as prescribed under Section 22-A hereof.
explanation: A self-employed member with zero income in a month is excused from paying for that month — the counterpart of Sec. 11 for employees. He may still pay voluntarily under the separated-employee rules, but he cannot later backfill skipped months (no retroactive payment, except as Sec. 22-A allows). Practical application: seasonal earners (farmers, fishermen, project-based professionals) should plan voluntary payments around the benefit-qualifying windows rather than assuming they can catch up later. Exam point: pair Sec. 11-A with Sec. 22-A (quarterly SE remittance, no retroactive payment).

verbatim: Dependents — The dependents shall be the following: (1) The legal spouse entitled by law to receive support from the member; (2) The legitimate, legitimated or legally adopted, and illegitimate child who is unmarried, not gainfully employed, and has not reached twenty-one (21) years of age, or if over twenty-one (21) years of age, he is congenitally or while still a minor has been permanently incapacitated and incapable of self-support, physically or mentally; and (3) The parent who is receiving regular support from the member.
explanation: Dependents are a closed list: the legal spouse entitled to support, each qualifying child (legitimate, legitimated, legally adopted, or illegitimate — unmarried, not gainfully employed, under 21, or incapacitated since minority), and a parent receiving regular support. This definition feeds the dependents' pension (Sec. 12-A) and the beneficiary ladder (Sec. 8(k)). Practical application: HR dependent declarations and SSS beneficiary records must be kept current — an unreported dependent cannot draw a dependents' pension. Exam point: illegitimate children ARE dependents and can be primary beneficiaries, but at 50% of a legitimate child's share when legitimate children exist (Sec. 8(k)).

verbatim: Beneficiaries — The dependent spouse until he or she remarries, the dependent legitimate, legitimated or legally adopted, and illegitimate children, who shall be the primary beneficiaries of the member: Provided, That the dependent illegitimate children shall be entitled to fifty percent (50%) of the share of the legitimate, legitimated or legally adopted children: Provided, further, That in the absence of the dependent legitimate, legitimated or legally adopted children of the member, his/her dependent illegitimate children shall be entitled to one hundred percent (100%) of the benefits. In their absence, the dependent parents who shall be the secondary beneficiaries of the member. In the absence of all the foregoing, any other person designated by the member as his/her secondary beneficiary.
explanation: The beneficiary ladder has three rungs: primary (dependent spouse until remarriage + dependent children), secondary (dependent parents), and designated secondary (any person the member designates, only if no primary or secondary exists). The illegitimate-child sharing rule is heavily tested: 50% of a legitimate child's share when legitimate children concur, 100% when they do not. The spouse's status ends on remarriage. Practical application: members should file and update designations; claims processors apply this ladder strictly in death (Sec. 13) and survivor-pension (Secs. 12-B(d), 13-A(c)) cases. Remember: Aguas adds the dependency proof requirement for the spouse — legitimate marriage alone is not enough.

verbatim: Average monthly salary credit — The result obtained by dividing the sum of the last sixty (60) monthly salary credits immediately preceding the semester of contingency by sixty (60), or the result obtained by dividing the sum of all the monthly salary credits paid prior to the semester of contingency by the number of monthly contributions paid in the same period, whichever is greater: Provided, That the injury or sickness which caused the disability shall be deemed as the permanent disability for the purpose of computing the average monthly salary credit.
explanation: The AMSC is the average of the member's monthly salary credits, computed two ways with the HIGHER result controlling: (1) last 60 MSCs before the semester of contingency divided by 60, or (2) all MSCs paid before the semester of contingency divided by the number of contributions. Since the pension formulas (Sec. 12) are percentages of AMSC, higher and more consistent lifetime credits mean higher pensions. Practical application: voluntary members choosing an MSC are effectively choosing their future AMSC inputs — a low declared MSC today depresses the pension base. Remember: always compute both and take the greater.

verbatim: Monthly Pension. — (a) The monthly pension shall be the highest of the following amounts: (1) The sum of the following: (i) Three hundred pesos (P300.00); plus (ii) Twenty percent (20%) of the average monthly salary credit; plus (iii) Two percent (2%) of the average monthly salary credit for each credited year of service in excess of ten (10) years; or (2) Forty percent (40%) of the average monthly salary credit; or (3) One thousand pesos (P1,000.00): Provided, That the monthly pension shall in no case be paid for an aggregate amount of less than sixty (60) months. (b) Notwithstanding the preceding paragraph, the minimum pension shall be One thousand two hundred pesos (P1,200.00) for members with at least ten (10) credited years of service and Two thousand four hundred pesos (P2,400.00) for those with twenty (20) credited years of service: Provided, That the Commission, upon determination of actuarial soundness, may provide pension increase than the amounts specified herein. (c) Additional Benefit Allowance. — Pursuant to Memorandum from the Executive Secretary dated 22 February 2017, by authority of the President of the Republic of the Philippines, an additional monthly benefit allowance amounting to One thousand pesos (P1,000.00) shall be given to all retirement, death, and disability pensioners receiving monthly pensions in or after January two thousand seventeen (2017). The Commission may determine the grant of additional benefit allowance: Provided, That the actuarial soundness of the reserve fund shall be guaranteed. All other additional allowances to monthly pension subsequent to the Memorandum of the Executive Secretary dated February 22, 2017 shall be subject to the requirement of fund viability and sustainability as determined by the Commission based on the recommendations of the Office of the Chief Actuary guaranteeing the actuarial soundness of the grant of such allowances.
explanation: The monthly pension is the highest of three computations: (1) P300 + 20% of AMSC + 2% of AMSC per credited year of service beyond 10; (2) 40% of AMSC; or (3) a P1,000 floor — and it is guaranteed for at least 60 months in aggregate (the five-year guarantee that survivor provisions repeatedly invoke). Minimums: P1,200 (at least 10 CYS) and P2,400 (at least 20 CYS). The P1,000 additional allowance dates to January 2017 by executive authority and is codified here; later increases need actuarial soundness. Worked example: AMSC P15,000 with 25 CYS gives formula (1) = 300 + 3,000 + (15 × 300) = P7,800; formula (2) = P6,000; formula (3) = P1,000 — pension is P7,800 (before the allowance). Peso figures are as stated in RA 11199 — verify current pension amounts and any later increases with SSS before relying on them. Exam point: the 60-month guarantee is the bridge to Secs. 12-B(d) and 13-A(c).

verbatim: Dependents' Pension. — Where monthly pension is payable on account of death, permanent total disability or retirement, dependents' pension equivalent to ten percent (10%) of the monthly pension or Two hundred fifty pesos (P250.00), whichever is higher, shall also be paid for each dependent child conceived on or before the date of the contingency but not exceeding five (5), beginning with the youngest and without substitution: Provided, That where there are legitimate and illegitimate children, the former shall be preferred.
explanation: Each qualifying dependent child adds 10% of the monthly pension (minimum P250) on top of the retirement, death, or permanent-total-disability pension. Limits: conceived on or before the contingency date, maximum five children, youngest first, no substitution — and legitimate children are preferred over illegitimate ones in filling the five slots. Practical application: a retiree's monthly check is pension + (dependents' pensions), so dependent declarations directly affect the payout; children conceived after the contingency are excluded. Remember: five children max, P250 floor per child, and this add-on attaches only to monthly pensions for death, permanent total disability, or retirement.

verbatim: Retirement Benefits. — (a) A member who has paid at least one hundred twenty (120) monthly contributions prior to the semester of retirement and who: (1) has reached the age of sixty (60) years and is already separated from employment or has ceased to be self-employed; or (2) has reached the age of sixty-five (65) years, shall be entitled for as long as he lives to the monthly pension: Provided, That he shall have the option to receive his first eighteen (18) monthly pensions in lump sum discounted at a preferential rate of interest to be determined by the SSS. (b) A covered member who is sixty (60) years old at retirement and who does not qualify for pension benefits under paragraph (a) above, shall be entitled to a lump sum benefit equal to the total contributions paid by him and on his behalf: Provided, That he is separated from employment and is not continuing payment of contributions to the SSS on his own. (c) The monthly pension shall be suspended upon the reemployment or resumption of self-employment of a retired member who is less than sixty-five (65) years old. He shall again be subject to Section Eighteen and his employer to Section Nineteen of this Act. (d) Upon the death of the retired member, his primary beneficiaries as of the date of his retirement shall be entitled to receive the monthly pension: Provided, That if he has no primary beneficiaries and he dies within sixty (60) months from the start of his monthly pension, his secondary beneficiaries shall be entitled to a lump sum benefit equivalent to the total monthly pensions corresponding to the balance of the five-year guaranteed period, excluding the dependents' pension. (e) The monthly pension of a member who retires after reaching age sixty (60) shall be the higher of either: (1) the monthly pension computed at the earliest time he could have retired had he been separated from employment or ceased to be self-employed plus all adjustments thereto; or (2) the monthly pension computed at the time when he actually retires.
explanation: Retirement has two doors: optional at 60 (with 120 contributions AND separation/cessation of self-employment) and mandatory at 65 (120 contributions; separation not required). With 120 contributions the prize is a lifetime monthly pension, with an option to take the first 18 months as a discounted lump sum. At 60 without 120 contributions, the member gets only a lump sum equal to total contributions paid (and must stop paying). Reemployment before 65 suspends the pension and restarts coverage. Death of a retiree passes the monthly pension to primary beneficiaries as of the retirement date; if there are none and death occurs within 60 months, secondary beneficiaries get the balance of the five-year guarantee as a lump sum (excluding dependents' pensions). Late retirees get the higher of the earliest-possible or actual-retirement computation. Practical application: the 120-contribution line is the most important number in retirement planning — voluntary continuation (Sec. 11) exists precisely to cross it. Remember: 60 needs separation, 65 does not.

verbatim: Death Benefits. — Upon the death of a member who has paid at least thirty-six (36) monthly contributions prior to the semester of death, his primary beneficiaries shall be entitled to the monthly pension: Provided, That if he has no primary beneficiaries, his secondary beneficiaries shall be entitled to a lump sum benefit equivalent to thirty-six (36) times the monthly pension. If he has not paid the required thirty-six (36) monthly contributions, his primary or secondary beneficiaries shall be entitled to a lump sum benefit equivalent to the monthly pension times the number of monthly contributions paid to the SSS or twelve (12) times the monthly pension, whichever is higher.
explanation: Death benefits turn on two questions: (1) did the member pay at least 36 contributions before the semester of death, and (2) are there primary beneficiaries? With 36+ contributions: primary beneficiaries draw the monthly pension; if none, secondary beneficiaries get a lump sum of 36 × monthly pension. Below 36 contributions: whoever qualifies (primary or secondary) gets a lump sum of (monthly pension × contributions paid) or 12 × monthly pension, whichever is higher. Practical application: claims processors must first count contributions, then apply the Sec. 8(k) ladder as refined by Aguas (spouse must prove dependency; only legitimate, legitimated, legally adopted, or illegitimate children qualify — informal adoptees do not). Remember the ladder: 36+ and primary → pension; 36+ without primary → 36× lump sum; below 36 → contributions× or 12×, higher.

verbatim: Permanent Disability Benefits. — (a) Upon the permanent total disability of a member who has paid at least thirty-six (36) monthly contributions prior to the semester of disability, he shall be entitled to the monthly pension: Provided, That if he has not paid the required thirty-six (36) monthly contributions, he shall be entitled to a lump sum benefit equivalent to the monthly pension times the number of monthly contributions paid to the SSS or twelve (12) times the monthly pension, whichever is higher. A member who (1) has received a lump sum benefit; and (2) is reemployed or has resumed self-employment not earlier than one (1) year from the date of his disability shall again be subject to compulsory coverage and shall be considered a new member. (b) The monthly pension and dependents' pension shall be suspended upon the reemployment or resumption of self-employment or the recovery of the disabled member from his permanent total disability or his failure to present himself for examination at least once a year upon notice by the SSS. (c) Upon the death of the permanent total disability pensioner, his primary beneficiaries as of the date of disability shall be entitled to receive the monthly pension: Provided, That if he has no primary beneficiaries and he dies within sixty (60) months from the start of his monthly pension, his secondary beneficiaries shall be entitled to a lump sum benefit equivalent to the total monthly pensions corresponding to the balance of the five-year guaranteed period excluding the dependents' pension. (d) The following disabilities shall be deemed permanent total: (1) Complete loss of sight of both eyes; (2) Loss of two limbs at or above the ankle or wrists; (3) Permanent complete paralysis of two limbs; (4) Brain injury resulting to incurable imbecility or insanity; and (5) Such cases as determined and approved by the SSS. (e) If the disability is permanent partial, and such disability occurs before thirty-six (36) monthly contributions have been paid prior to the semester of disability, the benefit shall be such percentage of the lump sum benefit described in the preceding paragraph with due regard to the degree of disability as the Commission may determine. (f) If the disability is permanent partial and such disability occurs after thirty-six (36) monthly contributions have been paid prior to the semester of disability, the benefit shall be the monthly pension for permanent total disability payable not longer than the period designated in the following schedule: one thumb 10 months; one index finger 8; one middle finger 6; one ring finger 5; one little finger 3; one big toe 6; one hand 39; one arm 50; one foot 31; one leg 46; one ear 10; both ears 20; hearing of one ear 10; hearing of both ears 50; sight of one eye 25. (g) The percentage degree of disability which is equivalent to the ratio that the designated number of months of compensability bears to seventy-five (75), rounded to the next higher integer, shall not be additive for distinct, separate and unrelated permanent partial disabilities, but shall be additive for deteriorating and related permanent partial disabilities, to a maximum of one hundred percent (100%), in which case, the member shall be deemed as permanently totally disabled. (h) In case of permanent partial disability, the monthly pension benefit shall be given in lump sum if it is payable for less than twelve (12) months. (i) For the purpose of adjudicating retirement, death and permanent total disability pension benefits, contributions shall be deemed paid for the months during which the member received partial disability pension: Provided, That such contributions shall be based on his last contribution prior to his disability. (j) Should a member who is on partial disability pension retire or die, his disability pension shall cease upon his retirement or death.
explanation: Disability mirrors death's 36-contribution line: permanent total disability with 36+ contributions earns the monthly pension (plus dependents' pension); below 36, a lump sum of (pension × contributions) or 12× pension, higher. A lump-sum recipient who returns to work at least one year after disability re-enters compulsory coverage as a new member. The pension suspends on reemployment, recovery, or skipping the annual SSS medical exam. Death of a disability pensioner follows the same 60-month survivor rule as retirees. Permanent total disabilities are the five listed cases (both eyes, two limbs, two-limb paralysis, brain injury causing incurable imbecility/insanity, SSS-approved cases). Permanent partial disability uses the statutory schedule (months of pension per body part, e.g. one arm 50, one leg 46, one hand 39, sight of one eye 25); the degree (months ÷ 75, rounded up) aggregates only for deteriorating and related disabilities up to 100%, which converts the case to permanent total. Schedule awards under 12 months are paid in lump sum; months on partial disability pension count as paid contributions (at the last rate) toward later retirement/death/PTD claims; and the partial pension stops on retirement or death. Ortega v. SSC is the companion case: total permanent disability is adjudicated on SSS medical findings and substantial evidence, and SSS benefits are conceptually distinct from Labor Code compensation. Remember: 36/12× structure parallels Sec. 13 exactly.

verbatim: Funeral Benefit. — A funeral grant equivalent to Twelve thousand pesos (P12,000.00) shall be paid, in cash or in kind, to help defray the cost of funeral expenses upon the death of a member, including permanently totally disabled member or retiree.
explanation: The statute sets a P12,000 funeral grant payable on the death of any member, including a permanent-total-disability pensioner or retiree. CURRENT RULE (supersedes the peso amount): under SSS Circular No. 2023-009, effective 20 October 2023, the benefit is variable from P20,000 to P60,000 where the member paid at least 36 contributions (scaled to contributions and AMSC), and fixed at P12,000 where the member paid at least 1 but fewer than 36. It is paid to whoever proves the funeral expense (claimant files online via My.SSS if an SSS member, over the counter otherwise). Practical application: funeral claims are the fastest SSS death-related payout and are separate from — and additional to — death benefits under Sec. 13. Exam point: always pair the statutory P12,000 with the Circular 2023-009 update; a question asking the 'current' amount wants P20,000–P60,000/P12,000.

sourceRefs.section: Current amounts; Circular No. 2023-009, eff. 20 Oct 2023

verbatim: Sickness Benefit. — (a) A member who has paid at least three (3) monthly contributions in the twelve-month period immediately preceding the semester of sickness or injury and is confined therefor for more than three (3) days in a hospital or elsewhere with the approval of the SSS, shall, for each day of compensable confinement or a fraction thereof, be paid by his employer, or the SSS, if such person is unemployed or self-employed, a daily sickness benefit equivalent to ninety percent (90%) of his average daily salary credit, subject to the following conditions: (1) In no case shall the daily sickness benefit be paid longer than one hundred twenty (120) days in one (1) calendar year, nor shall any unused portion of the one hundred twenty (120) days of sickness benefit granted under this section be carried forward and added to the total number of compensable days allowable in the subsequent year; (2) The daily sickness benefit shall not be paid for more than two hundred forty (240) days on account of the same confinement; and (3) The employee member shall notify his employer of the fact of his sickness or injury within five (5) calendar days after the start of his confinement unless such confinement is in a hospital or the employee became sick or was injured while working or within the premises of the employer in which case, notification to the employer is not necessary: Provided, That if the member is unemployed or self-employed, he shall directly notify the SSS of his confinement within five (5) calendar days after the start thereof unless such confinement is in a hospital in which case notification is also not necessary: Provided, further, That in cases where notification is necessary, the confinement shall be deemed to have started not earlier than the fifth day immediately preceding the date of notification. (b) The compensable confinement shall begin on the first day of sickness, and the payment of such allowances shall be promptly made by the employer every regular payday or on the fifteenth and last day of each month, and similarly in the case of direct payment by the SSS, for as long as such allowances are due and payable: Provided, That such allowance shall begin only after all sick leaves of absence with full pay to the credit of the employee member shall have been exhausted. (c) One hundred percent (100%) of the daily benefits provided in the preceding paragraph shall be reimbursed by the SSS to said employer upon receipt of satisfactory proof of such payment and legality thereof: Provided, That the employer has notified the SSS of the confinement within five (5) calendar days after receipt of the notification from the employee member: Provided, further, That if the notification to the SSS is made by the employer beyond five (5) calendar days after receipt of the notification from the employee member, said employer shall be reimbursed only for each day of confinement starting from the tenth calendar day immediately preceding the date of notification to the SSS: Provided, finally, That the SSS shall reimburse the employer or pay the unemployed member only for confinement within the one-year period immediately preceding the date the claim for benefit or reimbursement is received by the SSS, except confinement in a hospital in which case the claim for benefit or reimbursement must be filed within one (1) year from the last day of confinement. (d) Where the employee member has given the required notification but the employer fails to notify the SSS of the confinement or to file the claim for reimbursement within the period prescribed in this section resulting in the reduction of the benefit or denial of the claim, such employer shall have no right to recover the corresponding daily allowance he advanced to the employee member as required in this section. (e) The claim of reimbursement shall be adjudicated by the SSS within a period of two (2) months from receipt thereof: Provided, That should no payment be received by the employer within one (1) month after the period prescribed herein for adjudication, the reimbursement shall thereafter earn simple interest of one percent (1%) per month until paid. (f) The provisions regarding the notification required of the member and the employer as well as the period within which the claim for benefit or reimbursement may be filed shall apply to all claims filed with the SSS.
explanation: Sickness benefit = 90% of average daily salary credit per day of compensable confinement, for members with at least 3 contributions in the 12 months before the semester of sickness, confined more than 3 days. Caps: 120 days per calendar year (no carryover), 240 days for the same confinement. The notice chain is the exam favorite: employee notifies employer within 5 calendar days — UNLESS confined in a hospital or taken ill/injured while working or within the premises; unemployed/SE members notify SSS directly within 5 days (also excused for hospital confinement); late notice backdates the deemed start to only 5 days before notification. The employer advances payment every payday (after company sick leaves with full pay are exhausted) and gets 100% reimbursement — but only if it notifies SSS within 5 days of the employee's notice; late employer notice cuts reimbursement to days from the 10th day before SSS notification. If the employer was duly notified yet fails to notify SSS or file the reimbursement claim, causing reduction or denial, it cannot recover its advances from the employee. Claims prescribe in one year (hospital: one year from last day of confinement); SSS adjudicates reimbursement within 2 months, and delayed reimbursement earns 1% simple interest per month after a one-month grace. Practical application: payroll must calendar the 5-day notice both ways — most sickness disputes are notice failures, not eligibility failures. Remember: 3 contributions, >3 days confinement, 90% ADSC, 120/240 caps, 5-day notices, 1% interest.

verbatim: Maternity Leave Benefit. — A female member who has paid at least three (3) monthly contributions in the twelve-month period immediately preceding the semester of her childbirth or miscarriage shall be paid a daily maternity benefit equivalent to one hundred percent (100%) of her average daily salary credit for sixty (60) days or seventy-eight (78) days in case of caesarian delivery, subject to the following conditions: (a) That the employee shall have notified her employer of her pregnancy and the probable date of her childbirth, which notice shall be transmitted to the SSS in accordance with the rules and regulations it may provide; (b) The full payment shall be advanced by the employer within thirty (30) days from the filing of the maternity leave application; (c) That payment of daily maternity benefits shall be a bar to the recovery of sickness benefits provided by this Act for the same period for which daily maternity benefits have been received; (d) That the maternity benefits provided under this section shall be paid only for the first four (4) deliveries or miscarriages; (e) That the SSS shall immediately reimburse the employer of one hundred percent (100%) of the amount of maternity benefits advanced to the employee by the employer upon receipt of satisfactory proof of such payment and legality thereof; and (f) That if an employee member should give birth or suffer miscarriage without the required contributions having been remitted for her by her employer to the SSS, or without the latter having been previously notified by the employer of the time of the pregnancy, the employer shall pay to the SSS damages equivalent to the benefits which said employee member would otherwise have been entitled to.
explanation: As enacted, Sec. 14-A paid 100% of ADSC for 60 days (78 for caesarian), for the first 4 deliveries only, on at least 3 contributions in the 12 months before the semester of childbirth — with employer advance within 30 days of application and 100% SSS reimbursement. CURRENT RULE (supersedes paragraphs (d) and the day counts): RA No. 11210, the 105-Day Expanded Maternity Leave Law, effective 11 March 2019, grants 105 days for live childbirth (normal or caesarian), 60 days for miscarriage or emergency termination including stillbirth, plus 15 days (120 total) for solo parents — for EVERY instance regardless of frequency — with an option to allocate up to 7 days to the child's father or an alternate caregiver.
